The search is systematic, not random: list the factor pairs of c, apply the sign rules (for c > 0 both hidden numbers share the sign of b; for c < 0 they have opposite signs, with the larger carrying the sign of b), and pick the pair whose sum is b. When c has few factor pairs the search is seconds long; when no pair works — as for x² + x + 1 or x² + 25-style constants under squares — the trinomial is prime over the integers and saying so with an exhausted search is a complete answer. Three refinements belong here: removing a common factor first so the trinomial is in clean form (6x² + 15x + 9 → 3(2x² + 5x + 3) hands off to the general-trinomial node); handling c < 0 carefully since the signs of the hidden numbers then differ; and completing the work by re-expanding, because a wrong pair reproduces a wrong middle coefficient and the check catches it in one line. This method is the single most examined factorisation technique in ICSE Class 9, appearing standalone and inside every downstream application — equation solving, fraction simplification, and area problems.
steps: The product–sum search is factorisation's central trick: a trinomial x² + bx + c stores two hidden numbers — their product in the constant c and their sum in the middle coefficient b — and factoring is nothing more than…

The identity is the contract: (x + p)(x + q) = x² + (p + q)x + pq means the search always has exactly two conditions — find p, q with pq = c and p + q = b — and any pair meeting both conditions finishes the problem…

Signs are decided before numbers: when c > 0 the hidden numbers share a sign (both positive if b > 0, both negative if b < 0); when c < 0 they disagree, the larger magnitude carrying the sign of b; these three sentences…

The search is exhaustive but short: list the factor pairs of |c| (12 gives 1×12, 2×6, 3×4), attach signs by the rules, and read off the pair whose sum is b — with c prime the answer is forced, and with c composite the…

Exhaustion is a verdict, not a defeat: if every factor pair of c misses the sum b, the trinomial is prime over the integers — x² + 5x + 7 (pairs of 7: 1+7 = 8, −1−7 = −8) has no split, and stating that cleanly is full…
Verification closes every case: expand (x + p)(x + q) and confirm both the middle coefficient and the constant; a one-value substitution (x = 1 or x = −1 is easiest) is the second, independent guard.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., (x + 2)(x + 10) "because 2 × 10 = 20") reveals the misconception that matching the product alone completes the factorisation, missing that both conditions bind simultaneously — the sum test 2 + 10 = 12 ≠ 9 rejects the pair, and only 4…
remember: (Recall) State the identity that the product–sum search reverses, and factorise x² + 9x + 20.
(Reasoning) Explain, using the identity, why a trinomial x² + bx + c with c > 0 and b < 0 must split into two negative brackets, and factorise x² − 9x + 20 on that basis.
(Evaluate) Factorise (a) x² − 2x − 24 and (b) x² + 8x + 16, and for each state which sign rule decided the brackets. Verify both.

cards.title: The difference of squares is an algebraic identity stating that for any two…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The difference of squares is an algebraic identity stating that for any two real numbers (or algebraic expressions) a and b, a^2 - b^2 = (a+b)(a-b). It follows directly from the distributive law: (a+b)(a-b)=a(a-b)+b(a-b)=a^2-ab+ab-b^2=a^2-b^2. The identity is symmetric; the order of the factors does not matter. It applies whenever a polynomial can be written as the subtraction of two perfect squares — each term must be a square of a monomial (e.g., x^2, 9y^2, 16, 25a^4). Recognising perfect squares is the prerequisite skill: a term is a perfect square if its coefficient is a square number and each variable’s exponent is even. Once identified, the expression is factorised by taking the square roots of the two terms as a and b and writing (a+b)(a-b). This technique is a special case of factorisation by grouping (node) and precedes the sum/difference of cubes (node).
steps: The difference of squares identity turns a subtraction of two squares into a product of a sum and a difference, making many algebra problems instantly simpler.
Here is why: the product (a+b)(a-b) expands to a^2-b^2 because the middle terms -ab and +ab cancel.
This cancellation is the engine of the method — it removes the linear term entirely.
Consider the expression x^2-16.
Both x^2 and 16 are perfect squares: x^2=(x)^2 and 16=(4)^2.
Taking a=x and b=4 gives (x+4)(x-4).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., a^2-b^2=(a-b)^2) reveals the misconception that squaring a difference yields the same result — confusing (a-b)^2=a^2-2ab+b^2 with the difference of squares.
remember: State the algebraic identity for the difference of two squares.
Explain why x^2+25 cannot be factorised using the difference of squares identity over the real numbers.
Evaluate the factorisation: 36a^4-81b^2 = (6a^2+9b)(6a^2-9b). Is it fully factorised? Justify.

cards.title: The sum of cubes and difference of cubes are two special algebraic identities…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition:
The sum of cubes and difference of cubes are two special algebraic identities used to factorise expressions of the form a³ + b³ and a³ – b³ respectively. For any two algebraic quantities a and b (which may be numbers, variables, or more complex expressions), the identities are: - Sum of cubes: a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² – ab + b²)
- Difference of cubes: a³ – b³ = (a – b)(a² + ab + b²) These identities are derived by expanding the right‑hand sides and verifying that all cross terms cancel, leaving only the cubes. They are the cubic analogues of the difference of squares identity a² – b² = (a – b)(a + b) covered in the previous node. Recognising a sum or difference of cubes allows a polynomial of degree three to be broken into a linear factor and an irreducible quadratic factor (over the reals). This is essential for simplifying algebraic fractions, solving cubic equations, and performing polynomial division in later chapters. The quadratic factor a² ± ab + b² cannot be factorised further using real coefficients because its discriminant (±b)² – 4·1·b² = –3b² is negative unless b = 0. Mastery of these identities also supports the factorisation of higher‑degree polynomials by grouping terms into cubes.
steps: The sum and difference of cubes factorise into a linear term and a quadratic term that never splits further over real numbers.
Here is why: when you expand (a + b)(a² – ab + b²) you get a³ – a²b + ab² + a²b – ab² + b³ = a³ + b³; all middle terms cancel.
The same cancellation happens for (a – b)(a² + ab + b²) giving a³ – b³.
Consider the expression 27p³ + 64q³.
First, spot the cubes: 27p³ = (3p)³ and 64q³ = (4q)³.
So a = 3p, b = 4q.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² + ab + b²)) reveals the misconception that the quadratic factor always has a plus sign — confusing the pattern with the difference of squares where both signs are plus.
remember: State the factorised form of a³ + b³ and a³ – b³ using the standard identities.
Factorise completely: 8x³ + 27y³.
Factorise completely: 64a³ – 125b³.

cards.title: This node completes the factorisation toolkit with the three-term methods.
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: This node completes the factorisation toolkit with the three-term methods. A perfect square trinomial is an expression of the form a² + 2ab + b² or a² − 2ab + b², factorising as (a + b)² or (a − b)²; its identification test is three-way — first and last terms are exact squares, the connecting sign of the middle term is the bracket's sign, and the middle coefficient must equal exactly 2 × (root of first) × (root of last) — the middle-term check is what separates 4x² + 12x + 9 = (2x + 3)² from the near-miss 4x² + 13x + 9, which is not a perfect square. A general trinomial ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 1 is factorised over the integers by splitting the middle term: find integers r and s with rs = ac (the product of the outer coefficients) and r + s = b, rewrite bx as rx + sx, and finish by grouping: ax² + rx + sx + c. The product condition generalises the unit-leading case (there ac was simply c), and the method's correctness rests on the grouping machinery of the earlier node. Two habits guard the work: take out any common factor first so the coefficients are smallest (6x² + 21x + 15 → 3(2x² + 7x + 5) before splitting), and re-expand at the end — a wrong split reproduces a wrong middle term and the check catches it in one line. When no integer pair meets both conditions, the trinomial is prime over the integers and the exhausted search is stated as the verdict. The method choice table for any three-term expression: check perfect square first (cheap, one test), then split; expressions failing both, after HCF cleaning, are prime.
steps: The three-term expressions close the toolkit with two methods in a fixed order — the perfect-square test first, and when it fails, the middle-term split — and the pair covers every factorable trinomial the ICSE paper…
The perfect-square test is one cheap question before any search: are the outer terms squares and is the middle coefficient exactly twice their roots' product?

In 9a² − 30ab + 25b² the roots are 3a and 5b and 2 × 3a × 5b = 30ab ✓, so the answer is (3a − 5b)² with the middle sign copied — but in 4x² + 13x + 9 the roots 2x and 3 predict 12x, the test fails, and the expression…

The split's two conditions are the ac-generalisation of the old product–sum: find r, s with r·s = ac and r + s = b; in 6x² + 17x + 5, ac = 30 and b = 17 select 15 and 2, so the middle term divides into 15x + 2x.

The finish is always the grouping machine: 6x² + 15x + 2x + 5 = 3x(2x + 5) + 1(2x + 5) = (2x + 5)(3x + 1) — the split manufactures the four-term form, grouping collapses it, and the student who owns the earlier node…

Signs in the split obey the same three rules as before: c positive means r, s share a sign (the sign of b); c negative means opposite signs with the larger magnitude carrying b's sign — but now the product watched is…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., claiming 25x² + 39x + 16 = (5x + 4)² − x and calling it factored) reveals the misconception that proximity to a pattern licenses its use, missing that an identity is exact — the middle coefficient must match to the unit, or the method is…
remember: (Recall) State the two perfect-square trinomial identities and factorise 25x² + 40x + 16 after confirming it qualifies.
(Reasoning) Explain why splitting the middle term of ax² + bx + c uses the product ac rather than c, connecting your explanation to the expansion of (mx + n)(px + q).
(Evaluate) Factorise (a) 49m² − 84m + 36 [perfect square test first]; (b) 3x² + 14x + 8; (c) 4x² + 10x − 6? [clean first]. Verify (b) by expansion.

cards.title: Synthesis is the chapter's consolidation node: it assembles the seven methods…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Synthesis is the chapter's consolidation node: it assembles the seven methods — common factors, grouping, the unit-leading trinomial search, difference of squares, sum and difference of cubes, perfect-square trinomials, and the middle-term split — into a single decision pipeline governed by the ICSE examination conventions. The pipeline has a fixed opening move (extract the global HCF), a shape-reading middle (count terms, test square/cube status, check for groupable pairs or splittable trinomials), and a compulsory closing move (the completeness scan: every bracket re-tested until each is prime over the rationals). The examination culture of the chapter runs to three question families: direct factorisation ("factorise completely"), where the pipeline is the whole answer; factorisation in service, where the product is used to evaluate an arithmetic quantity (a³ − b³ at nearby cubes), simplify a ratio of expressions, or read off solutions of an equation set to zero; and structural problems, where factorisation reveals geometry (side lengths from areas) or number relationships (digit and age problems). Two habits distinguish full-credit work: writing the method's name or test before computing, and verifying by re-expansion or substitution before declaring the answer. The node's deeper claim is that method choice is not six-way guessing but a decision tree with at most two branches at each step — term count and pattern tests — and fluent students execute it in seconds.
steps: Factorisation mastery is not seven skills but one pipeline run at speed — extract the HCF, read the shape, apply the method, repeat inside every bracket, and stop only when the completeness scan certifies that nothing…

The opening move is invariable: take out the global HCF before any classification, because the classification changes — 3x² − 27 is not "prime-looking" but 3(x − 3)(x + 3); 16x⁵ + 54x² is not a cube problem but 2x²(2x +…

Shape-reading is a two-question cascade: count the terms (two terms → square test, then cube test; three terms → perfect-square test, then middle-term split; four terms → grouping, often after a manufactured split), and…

Factorisation in service is the exam's favourite frame: evaluate 101³ − 100³ = (1)(10201 + 10100 + 10000) = 30301; solve (x − 3)(x + 4) = 0 by the zero-product reading; recover a rectangle's sides from (x + 3)(x + 8) …
Verification is the mark-earning habit: re-expand the final answer or substitute one convenient value;
CISCE marking schemes credit the check line, and the habit catches the sign slips and missed HCFs that the completeness scan alone cannot.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., testing cubes before extracting the HCF on 16x⁵ + 54x²) reveals the misconception that method order is aesthetic, missing that the HCF's extraction changes which pattern is visible — the cube 8x³ + 27 only exists after 2x² comes out, so…
remember: (Recall) List the chapter's seven methods in the order you would test them, and state the one-line test that selects each.

cards.title: Simultaneous linear equations are two (or more) equations in the same two
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Simultaneous linear equations are two (or more) equations in the same two (or more) variables that must hold at once; a solution is an assignment of values to the variables satisfying every equation together. For a linear pair in x and y — each equation of the form ax + by = c with constant coefficients — the solution set is the answer to the geometric question of where the two straight lines meet: one common point (a consistent, independent system), no point (inconsistent, the lines parallel), or every point of one line (dependent, the equations are one line in two costumes). The chapter's toolkit has three engines: substitution (solve one equation for a variable, substitute into the other), elimination (scale the equations so one variable's coefficients cancel on addition or subtraction), and cross-multiplication (the determinant formula x = (b₁c₂ − b₂c₁)/(a₁b₂ − a₂b₁), y = (c₁a₂ − c₂a₁)/(a₁b₂ − a₂b₁) for the pair a₁x + b₁y = c₁, a₂x + b₂y = c₂), each with a domain of maximum efficiency — clear isolation, matching coefficients, and no-easy-coefficient systems respectively. The chapter's second half is word problems: translating a story — tickets and totals, ages now and then, fractions of amounts, two-digit numbers — into exactly two equations and letting the engines finish. Two disciplines govern everything: solutions are always checked in both original equations, and the method is always chosen by the shape of the coefficients, not by habit — the three engines compute the same answer, but only fast selection earns exam time.

cards.title: The substitution method solves a pair of simultaneous linear equations by using…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The substitution method solves a pair of simultaneous linear equations by using one equation to express one variable in terms of the other, and substituting that expression into the partner equation, producing a single linear equation in one variable that transposition then solves; the found value is back-substituted into the expression to recover the second variable, and the pair is verified in both original equations. For the system a₁x + b₁y = c₁, a₂x + b₂y = c₂, the method runs: solve the easier equation for the easier variable (a variable whose coefficient is ±1 is the prize), substitute, solve, back-substitute, verify. Its strategic home is the system where isolation is cheap — a variable already standing alone (y = 2x + 5), a coefficient of 1 or −1 (x − y = 9 gives x = y + 9 in one move), or a relation naturally phrased as "one quantity in terms of another" (the chocolate costs 20 more than the vanilla). Its weakness is symmetric systems with large or fractional coefficients, where isolating manufactures fractions that elimination handles more safely. Two disciplines separate full-credit work: the expression used for substitution is stated explicitly before replacing ("from (1): y = 2x + 1"), and the final check runs in both original equations — the substituted equation alone cannot catch an algebra slip made during the substitution itself, since the slip contaminates every equation it touched.

cards.title: The elimination method solves a pair of simultaneous linear equations by…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The elimination method solves a pair of simultaneous linear equations by scaling one or both equations so that one variable's coefficients become equal (or equal and opposite), then adding or subtracting the equations to make that variable vanish, leaving one linear equation in the surviving variable; the found value is back-substituted into an original equation, and the pair is verified in both. For the system a₁x + b₁y = c₁, a₂x + b₂y = c₂, the elimination multipliers for killing y are the other equation's y-coefficient applied to each equation: multiply the first by b₂ and the second by b₁; the y-coefficients become equal in size, and subtraction removes y when the signs agree, addition when they oppose. The method's strategic home is the symmetric-coefficient system — nothing isolates cheaply, but coefficients match or nearly match (4x + 7y = 2 and 4x − 3y = 10 share the 4x) — and its showcase trick is the mirrored system Ax + By = P, Bx + Ay = Q, where adding the equations yields x + y and subtracting yields x − y, turning even two-digit coefficients into a two-line solve. Its weakness is a system with a ready-made isolation, which belongs to substitution; otherwise elimination handles every linear pair, at the price of the required multiplications. Three disciplines govern full-credit work: the scalings are written explicitly ("multiply (1) by 5 and (2) by 4"), the merge is written as a bracketed subtraction or addition (subtracting a negative term adds it), and the verification runs in both ORIGINAL equations — the scaled copies cannot see a slip made while producing them.

cards.title: The cross-multiplication method solves the standard system a₁x + b₁y = c₁…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The cross-multiplication method solves the standard system a₁x + b₁y = c₁, a₂x + b₂y = c₂ by direct formula. Define the denominator D = a₁b₂ − a₂b₁. Then, provided D ≠ 0, the solution is x = (b₂c₁ − b₁c₂)/D and y = (a₁c₂ − a₂c₁)/D. Each numerator is a cross-pair product difference: for x, the second equation's y-coefficient times the first equation's constant, minus the reverse; for y, the same construction with the x-coefficients. The method is derived, not conjured: eliminating y by scaling (the elimination machinery) produces exactly D·x = b₂c₁ − b₁c₂, and eliminating x produces D·y = a₁c₂ − a₂c₁ — the formula is elimination performed once in symbols and reused forever. The denominator D is the system's decision quantity: D ≠ 0 means a unique solution; D = 0 means the left sides are proportional, so the system is dependent (infinitely many solutions, when the constants are proportional too) or inconsistent (none, when they are not) — the formula refuses to run exactly when the geometry refuses to cross. Cross-multiplication is the engine of choice for ugly coefficient systems — fractional or decimal coefficients, rows with no useful common factors — where substitution manufactures fractions and elimination's scaling invites sign slips, but the formula's two divisions are mechanical. The working discipline: compute and write D first (it also warns of the special cases), then the two numerators with every product visible, then reduce the fractions exactly and verify in both originals.

cards.title: A word problem in two unknowns is a story containing exactly two independent…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A word problem in two unknowns is a story containing exactly two independent constraint sentences about two quantities, and solving it is a four-stage discipline: (1) name the variables explicitly ("let the father's age be f years and the son's age be s years"); (2) translate each constraint sentence into a linear equation; (3) solve the system by any named engine; (4) verify and answer — check the pair in both equations AND re-read it into the story, then state the answer in the story's units and words, not as a bare coordinate pair. The chapter's standard problem families each carry their own translation conventions: number problems (sums and differences of two numbers); age problems (current ages related now, or after/before a stated number of years — "in 5 years" adds 5 to each age); money and ticket problems (a count equation and a value equation, with values as count × price); fraction problems (a fraction x/y whose value changes under "add 1 to the numerator" style operations); and two-digit number problems (tens digit t and units digit u make the number 10t + u; reversing makes 10u + t). Two translation principles govern everything: each sentence contributes ONE equation — relations like "twice as old" are equations, not extra unknowns — and the variables must be the quantities the question ASKS for, or explicitly linked to them, so the final sentence is a direct answer. The check stage is doubled by design: the algebraic check catches solving slips, and the story check catches translation slips — an answer that solves both equations but reads "the son is −4 years old" has exposed a translation error upstream.

cards.title: A pair of linear equations in two variables a_1x + b_1y = c_1 and a_2x + b_2y =…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A pair of linear equations in two variables a_1x + b_1y = c_1 and a_2x + b_2y = c_2 represents two straight lines in the Cartesian plane. The consistency of the system refers to whether the lines intersect (unique solution), coincide (infinitely many solutions), or are parallel (no solution). The algebraic test uses ratios of coefficients: - Unique solution (consistent and independent): (a_1)/(a_2) ≠ (b_1)/(b_2). The lines have different slopes and meet at exactly one point (x,y). - Infinitely many solutions (consistent and dependent): (a_1)/(a_2) = (b_1)/(b_2) = (c_1)/(c_2). The two equations are scalar multiples; they describe the same line. - No solution (inconsistent): (a_1)/(a_2) = (b_1)/(b_2) ≠ (c_1)/(c_2). The lines have equal slopes but different intercepts; they never meet. This concept extends the solving methods (substitution, elimination, cross‑multiplication) by telling you before you compute whether a solution exists and how many. It connects directly to the graphical interpretation taught in coordinate geometry and to word‑problem modelling where contradictory or redundant data appear.
steps: The consistency of a pair of linear equations is completely determined by the ratios of their coefficients — if the ratios of x‑ and y‑coefficients differ, the lines intersect once; if all three ratios match, the lines…
Here is why: each equation a_ix+b_iy=c_i can be rewritten as y = -(a_i)/(b_i)x + (c_i)/(b_i) (provided b_i≠0).
The slope is -(a_i)/(b_i).
Two lines have the same slope exactly when (a_1)/(a_2) = (b_1)/(b_2).
If, in addition, the intercepts (c_1)/(b_1) and (c_2)/(b_2) are equal, the lines are identical — this happens precisely when (a_1)/(a_2) = (b_1)/(b_2) = (c_1)/(c_2).
If the slopes match but intercepts differ, the lines are distinct parallels — no intersection.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “(a_1)/(a_2) = (b_1)/(b_2) = (c_1)/(c_2)”) reveals the misconception that equal ratios give a unique solution, confusing the condition for infinite solutions with that for a unique solution.

cards.title: Harder word problems are the translation families whose raw sentences do not…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Harder word problems are the translation families whose raw sentences do not hand over standard-form equations, and mastering them means owning three upgrade techniques that sit ON TOP of the four-stage discipline from. (1) The ratio-variable method: a sentence like "two quantities are in the ratio 3: 4" is translated as x = 3k and y = 4k with a single new parameter k, so the ratio constraint is consumed at birth and the remaining sentence supplies one linear equation in k; this beats writing y = (4/3)x, which drags fractions through the algebra. Changed-ratio problems ("after each receives 500, the ratio becomes 2: 3") simply shift both variables first and then equate the new ratio to the new parameter. (2) Rearrangement to standard form: coefficients arriving as fractions (x/2 + y/3 = 7) or decimals (0.3x + 0.4y = 5) are cleared by multiplying each equation by its LCM of denominators or by the power of ten that decimalises away — but the multiplication must hit EVERY term including the constant, or the equation is silently replaced by a different line. (3) Reducible systems: equations in reciprocals, such as 1/x + 1/y = 7/12, become linear the moment u = 1/x and v = 1/y are substituted; the solved pair (u, v) is inverted at the end to recover (x, y), and the inversion is legitimate only because x and y are nonzero. All three techniques converge on the same finish: a standard linear system solved by substitution, elimination, or cross-multiplication, verified in both equations and in the story. The classification machinery of remains in force underneath — a harder story can still turn out dependent (its second sentence merely restates the first) or inconsistent (its receipts collide), and recognising that IS part of the answer.

cards.title: The synthesis of the chapter is a single decision pipeline that routes any…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The synthesis of the chapter is a single decision pipeline that routes any simultaneous-equations task through five stages: (1) Translate — word sentences become equations via the family conventions (ages, money counts, digit place values, ratio parameters, denominator clearing, reciprocal substitution); pure systems skip straight to standard form a1x + b1y = c1. (2) Classify — compute D = a1b2 − a2b1 and consult the ratio test: D ≠ 0 promises exactly one solution; D = 0 with unequal constant ratios means no solution (write that verdict with the contradiction shown); D = 0 with equal constant ratios means infinitely many (exhibit the proportionality and, when asked, parametrise the solution family). (3) Select the engine — substitution when a variable arrives isolated or with coefficient 1; elimination when matching coefficients are one scaling away or when adding/subtracting kills a variable immediately; cross-multiplication as the one-formula route whose denominator doubles as the consistency diagnostic. (4) Solve with every intermediate line shown — ICSE awards method marks line by line. (5) Verify and answer — substitute into BOTH original equations, re-read the pair into the story (positive ages, whole tickets, digits 0–9), and close with a sentence carrying units. The pipeline is bidirectional in one place: when a k-parameter question fixes the TYPE (unique, none, infinite), the classification test runs FIRST and its ratio conditions generate the equation for k before any solving. Exam pattern awareness completes the synthesis: short-answer items ask for one solved pair or one k-value (1–2 marks); long items add translation and verification stages (3–4 marks); application items wrap the pipeline in a story worth 5–6, with marks typically split translation 2, solving 2, verification 2 — the pipeline's stages are literally the marking scheme's rows.

cards.title: An index (plural: indices; also called an exponent or power) records repeated…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: An index (plural: indices; also called an exponent or power) records repeated multiplication: for a positive integer n and any real base a, the symbol aⁿ means the product of n copies of a — a·a·…·a (n times) — where a is the base and n the index; a itself is called the base quantity and aⁿ "the nth power of a". The chapter's engine is a set of five laws of indices, first established for positive integral indices: (1) Product law — aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ, because the m factors of aᵐ followed by the n factors of aⁿ make m + n factors altogether; (2) Quotient law — aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ for a ≠ 0, because n of the m factors cancel, leaving m − n; (3) Power of a power — (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ, because n copies of "m factors" make mn factors; (4) Power of a product — (ab)ⁿ = aⁿbⁿ, because each of the n bracketed copies contributes one a and one b; (5) Power of a quotient — (a/b)ⁿ = aⁿ/bⁿ for b ≠ 0, by the same counting on the fraction. Two structural facts ride with the laws: the laws speak only about INDICES — the base is preserved across each law, which is why "same base" is the entry ticket to laws 1–3 — and composite bases such as 4, 8, or 9 become law-eligible the moment they are re-expressed as powers of a common base (4 = 2², 8 = 2³, 9 = 3²), the chapter's most reused conversion. The laws are theorems, not conventions: each is proved by expanding the products and counting factors, and every later extension — zero, negative, and fractional indices in the nodes ahead — is designed so that these five laws continue to hold without exception.
steps: Indices are a counting machine for repeated multiplication: aⁿ counts n identical factors, and the five laws are nothing more than careful counts — read each law as a sentence about factors once, and you will never mix…
The product law is the mother law: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ because the factors pile up — 2³ × 2⁴ is (2·2·2)(2·2·2·2), five plus four... three plus four factors: seven 2's, i.e. 2⁷.
The indices ADD because the factors CONCATENATE.
The matching trap: a different base cannot share the law — 2³ × 3² has no fusion available; the factors are of different kinds and stay separate.
The quotient law subtracts because cancelling removes factors: 2⁶ ÷ 2⁴ = (2·2·2·2·2·2)/(2·2·2·2), the four bottom 2's cancel four top 2's, leaving 2².
The index arithmetic m − n is literally "how many factors survive".
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 2⁶ × 2³ = 2¹⁸ "multiplying the indices") reveals the misconception that index operations follow the visible multiplication sign, missing that the law maps MULTIPLICATION of powers to ADDITION of indices — factors concatenate (six 2's…
remember: (Recall) State the five laws of indices (positive integral indices) with their exact conditions, and compute 2⁶ × 2³ and (10²)³ using the correct laws.
(Reasoning) Prove the product law aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ by expanding factors, then use it to compute 3⁴ × 3⁵ without expanding fully, and verify the result by multiplication.
(Evaluate) Simplify (x³)² × x⁴ ÷ x⁵ to a single power of x, naming the law used at each step, and check the result at x = 2.

cards.title: The zero index and negative indices extend powers beyond factor-counting…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The zero index and negative indices extend powers beyond factor-counting, and both are DEFINED by the requirement that the five laws of continue to hold. For any nonzero base a: a⁰ = 1, because the quotient law demands aᵐ ÷ aᵐ = aᵐ⁻ᵐ = a⁰ while cancellation shows aᵐ ÷ aᵐ = 1 — the only value of a⁰ consistent with both is 1. a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ, because aⁿ × a⁻ⁿ must equal aⁿ⁺⁽⁻ⁿ⁾ = a⁰ = 1, making a⁻ⁿ the multiplicative inverse (reciprocal) of aⁿ. Three consequences do daily work: 1/a⁻ⁿ = aⁿ (a negative index in a denominator is a positive index in the numerator); (a/b)⁻ⁿ = (b/a)ⁿ — inverting the base fraction flips the sign of the index, so (2/3)⁻³ = (3/2)³ = 27/8; and moving any factor across a fraction line flips its index sign, the bookkeeping rule that makes multi-term simplification mechanical. With these definitions the five laws now hold for ALL integer indices, positive, zero, and negative — e.g. 2⁵ × 2⁻³ = 2² = 4, verifying directly as 32 × 1/8 = 4. Two boundary guards: the base must be nonzero (0⁰ and 0 to a negative index are undefined — 0 has no reciprocal), and the sign of the ANSWER is unaffected by the sign of the index: (−2)⁻³ = 1/(−2)³ = −1/8, the negative sign belonging to the base and surviving the reciprocal. The same definitions make standard form (scientific notation) natural: 0.0004 = 4 × 10⁻⁴, because each division by ten removes one power of ten — the negative index counting the decimal places.
steps: Zero and negative indices are not new rules — they are the OLD rules refusing to break: define a⁰ as whatever makes aᵐ ÷ aᵐ = a⁰ true, define a⁻ⁿ as whatever makes aⁿ × a⁻ⁿ = a⁰ true, and the laws themselves hand you…
The zero derivation, done slowly: 5³ ÷ 5³ is 125/125 = 1 by cancellation, and 5³⁻³ = 5⁰ by the quotient law — one quantity, two descriptions, so 5⁰ = 1.
Same for every nonzero base: the index has run out of factors, and "no factors" multiplies to the empty product, 1.
The exclusion of 0⁰ is not pedantry: 0³ ÷ 0³ is 0/0, which is undefined, so no law forces any value and none is assigned.
The negative derivation: 5² × 5⁻² must equal 5⁰ = 1 by the product law, so 5⁻² is the number that multiplies 25 to give 1 — namely 1/25.
In general a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ: the minus sign in the index is a RECYCLING SIGN, sending the factor to the other side of the fraction bar. The flip rules are the working tools: 1/2⁻⁵ = 2⁵;
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., (−1)⁻³ = 1 "because negative index means positive answer") reveals the misconception that the index sign controls the answer's sign, missing that the INDEX sign controls POSITION (numerator or denominator) while the BASE's sign controls…
remember: (Recall) Define a⁰ and a⁻ⁿ precisely with their conditions, and evaluate: 9⁰, 5⁻², 2⁻⁴, (1/10)⁰, and (−1)⁻³.
(Reasoning) Derive a⁰ = 1 from the quotient law and a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ from the product law, and explain precisely why 0⁰ and 0⁻² are left undefined while 0³ is fine.
(Evaluate) Simplify (3⁻² × 3⁴) ÷ 3⁻¹ to a whole number, showing the index chain, and verify by converting each power to a fraction first.

cards.title: For a positive real base a and positive integer n…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: For a positive real base a and positive integer n, the fractional index a^(1/n) is DEFINED as the nth root of a — the number whose nth power is a — because the power-of-power law demands (a^(1/n))ⁿ = a^(1/n × n) = a¹ = a, and only the nth root satisfies that. The general rational index is then a^(m/n) = (a^(1/n))ᵐ = (aᵐ)^(1/n) — "nth root first, then mth power", or "mth power first, then nth root"; the two readings agree (both are the laws forced), and the root-first route is almost always lighter arithmetic. Negative rational indices keep the reciprocal meaning: a^(−p/q) = 1/a^(p/q), so 25^(−1/2) = 1/5 and (8/27)^(−2/3) = (27/8)^(2/3) = 9/4. With these definitions the five laws now hold for ALL rational indices, e.g. 5^(1/2) × 5^(3/2) = 5² = 25 — directly, √5 × √5 = 5 ✓. Boundary conditions matter from this node on: even roots (n even, as in a^(1/2)) exist only for a ≥ 0 in the real numbers — no real number squares to −4 — while odd roots exist for every real a; this course takes positive bases throughout the law-work, so every base below is positive unless a diagnostic asks the boundary question. The computational strategy the definitions license is the common-base conversion in reverse: since 8 = 2³, we have 8^(2/3) = 2² = 4 without touching a root sign — writing bases as exact powers (8 = 2³, 9 = 3², 16 = 2⁴, 25 = 5², 27 = 3³, 32 = 2⁵, 125 = 5³) turns fractional-index evaluation into ordinary index addition and multiplication, and that conversion is the node's central skill.
steps: Fractional indices complete the design: if the laws are to survive at exponent 1/2, then 4^(1/2) must square to 4 — so it must BE 2; every rational index is thus a root wearing the laws' uniform, and the whole node is…

The reading rule, stated once: the DENOMINATOR is the root, the NUMERATOR is the power — a^(m/n) = (root_n of a) to the m. Route order is free ((aᵐ)^(1/n) is the same number), but root-first is cheaper: 27^(2/3) = (3)²…
The two readings are themselves a law-check: (a^(1/n))ᵐ = ((aᵐ)^(1/n)) because both equal a^(m/n) by the power-of-power law. Negative fractional indices stay reciprocals: 25^(−1/2) = 1/√25 = 1/5;

The sign flip continues to mean position, never the answer's sign — and the even-root condition (base ≥ 0) now guards the base: there is no √(−4) in the reals, so (−4)^(1/2) is undefined even though (−8)^(1/3) = −2 is…
The evaluation strategy is exact-power recognition: 8^(2/3) = (2³)^(2/3) = 2² = 4; 16^(−3/4) = 2^(−3) = 1/8; 125^(4/3) = 5⁴ = 625.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 16^(3/4) = 16 × 3/4 = 12 "multiplying the base by the fraction") reveals the misconception that the fractional index scales the base linearly, missing that the index is an EXPONENT instruction — denominator = root, numerator = power …
remember: (Recall) Define a^(1/n) and a^(m/n) as the laws force, state the even-root condition, and evaluate: 4^(1/2), 27^(1/3), 25^(−1/2), 16^(3/4), and 32^(2/5).
(Reasoning) Show that the two readings of a^(m/n) — (a^(1/n))ᵐ and (aᵐ)^(1/n) — must agree, by evaluating 64^(2/3) BOTH ways with full working, and explain why root-first is the….
(Evaluate) Evaluate (8/27)^(2/3) and (8/27)^(−2/3), and explain how the power of a quotient law connects the two computations.

cards.title: Multi-law simplification is the disciplined assembly of every tool from the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Multi-law simplification is the disciplined assembly of every tool from the previous nodes — the five laws, zero and negative indices, fractional indices, and common-base conversion — into a single evaluation of a compound expression. The canonical strategy has three stages. (1) Convert: rewrite every numerical base as a power of the smallest common base (16 = 2⁴, 25 = 5², 27 = 3³, 125 = 5³); literals keep their letters. (2) Chain: apply the laws so that the whole expression becomes ONE base raised to ONE accumulated index — brackets multiply indices, products add them, quotients subtract them, with fractions of indices added and subtracted by ordinary fraction arithmetic. (3) Present: convert the final power to the conventional form — a whole number when exact (2³ = 8), a positive-index expression when negative (2⁻⁵ = 1/32), a surd form when fractional (2^(3/2) = 2√2). The presentation convention of CISCE marking is "positive indices", so stage 3 is a marked step, not a decoration. Two structural principles govern the chain: the laws act ONLY on factors connected by multiplication and division — a sum inside a bracket must be evaluated as arithmetic FIRST ((2⁻¹ + 2⁻²) is 1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4, not 2⁻³) — and the chain inherits the left-to-right order of any equal-precedence run, which is why the signed index sum must be written in the expression's own order before evaluating. Mastering the pipeline converts expressions of eight or ten factors from intimidating to mechanical: each factor contributes its signed index to one pot, and the pot is emptied once.
steps: A long index expression is one bookkeeping problem, not many: convert every base to a common stock, let each factor deposit its signed index, and settle the account once — the discipline is in the order of operations…

Convert first, always: an expression mixing 8, 16, and 4 is unreadable until all three are powers of 2 — 8^(2/3) × 16^(−1/4) × 4^(5/4) is chaos in original dress and one line after conversion: 2² × 2⁻¹ × 2^(5/2) = 2^(2…

The stored conversion table (4, 8, 16, 32, 64 for 2; 9, 27, 81 for 3; 25, 125 for 5) is the pipeline's first tool, and conversions inside fractional indices obey the power-of-power law: 16^(−3/4) = (2⁴)^(−3/4) = 2⁻³.

Chain with the SIGNED SUM written out: for (2^(5/2) × 4^(−3/4) × 8^(1/6)), the conversion gives 2^(5/2) × 2^(−3/2) × 2^(1/2), and the full sum 5/2 − 3/2 + 1/2 = 3/2 is written BEFORE evaluating — the double negatives…
The result 2^(3/2) = 2√2 ≈ 2.828 is verifiable numerically: 5.657 × 0.354 × 1.414 ≈ 2.828 ✓.
Sums inside brackets are arithmetic first: (3⁻¹ − 3⁻²) is 1/3 − 1/9 = 2/9, and NO index law applies to the addition — the laws govern ×, ÷, and brackets-of-powers only.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 1 ÷ 3⁻³ evaluated as 1/27 "dividing by the fraction wrong... as division by three cubed") reveals the misconception that dividing by a reciprocal divides again, missing that ÷ 3⁻³ = ÷ (1/27) = × 27; in index language the divisor's index…

(Reasoning) Explain why conversion to a common base must precede any index chaining, and demonstrate the failure by attempting to chain 8^(2/3) × 4^(1/2) × 32^(−1/5) WITHOUT….
(Evaluate) Evaluate [6⁻¹ − (2/3)⁻¹]², showing the bracket-sum discipline, and explain why no index law may be applied inside the bracket.

cards.title: An exponential equation is an equation in which the unknown x sits in an INDEX…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: An exponential equation is an equation in which the unknown x sits in an INDEX — 2ˣ = 32, 3^(2x−1) = 1/27, (2/3)^x = 9/4 — and the Class 9 method solves the family where both sides can be written as powers of ONE common base. The governing principle is the equating of indices: if aˣ = aʸ with a > 0 and a ≠ 1, then x = y, because a fixed positive base other than 1 grows (a > 1) or decays (0 < a < 1) strictly and never repeats a value — each index produces exactly one output, so equal outputs force equal indices. The working procedure has three steps: (1) Convert both sides to powers of the common base, using the exact-power conversions (32 = 2⁵, 1/27 = 3⁻³, 9/4 = (3/2)², 0.5 = 2⁻¹, 25 = 5², 125 = 5³) and the flip rule for fraction bases ((4/9) = (2/3)²). (2) Tidy each side into ONE power using the laws: products add indices, quotients subtract them, brackets multiply them — 5^(2x) × 125 ÷ 25 becomes 5^(2x + 1). (3) Equate indices and solve the resulting linear equation in x; verify by substituting back into the ORIGINAL equation. Boundary conditions are part of the theory: the base a = 1 is excluded (1ˣ = 1 for every x, so 1ˣ = 1ʸ says nothing), a = 0 is excluded (0 to a negative index is undefined), and negative bases are excluded from the general method (their powers misbehave for fractional x) — this course solves equations with positive bases other than 1. When one side cannot be converted (2ˣ = 12 has no exact answer in this method), the honest Class 9 verdict is "not solvable exactly by this method" rather than an approximation.
steps: Exponential equations are the index laws run in reverse: instead of simplifying an expression to find its value, the value is known and the index is hunted — and the hunt succeeds exactly when both sides can be dressed…

The principle deserves its justification, not just its statement: 2¹ = 2, 2² = 4, 2³ = 8 — each step of the index raises the value, and no two steps give the same value; a strictly climbing (or, for fractions, strictly…

The conversions are the chapter's stored table used at speed: 1/27 = 3⁻³ (reciprocal, then cube); 9/4 = (3/2)² (quotient as a power of the flipped fraction); 0.25 = 2⁻² (decimal, then negative index); 6.25 = 5²·... 6.25…
A right side that resists every conversion (2ˣ = 12) ends the exact method honestly — the answer is "not solvable exactly at this level", not a guessed decimal.

Tidying one side is law-work: 5^(2x) × 125 ÷ 25 = 5^(2x) × 5³ ÷ 5² = 5^(2x + 1) — the whole left side is one power with one linear index expression; equations with factors on BOTH sides (9^(x+1) = 27ˣ) convert…

The linear finish is ordinary algebra: 2x − 1 = −3 gives x = −1; fractional answers are fully legitimate — 4ˣ = 1/8 becomes 2^(2x) = 2⁻³, so 2x = −3, x = −3/2 — and the verification substitutes into the ORIGINAL…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 3ˣ = 81 solved as x = 81/3 = 27) reveals the misconception that indices divide like coefficients, missing that the index is found by REWRITING the value in the base's currency (81 = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3, four factors) — division asks "how many…
remember: (Recall) State the equating-of-indices principle with its conditions, and solve 3ˣ = 81 and 2^(x−1) = 1/16.
(Reasoning) Justify the exclusion of base a = 1 from the equating principle with a concrete failed equation, and explain how the staircase picture (strictly rising for a > 1….
(Evaluate) Solve 2^(3x) × 2^(2x+1) = 64, naming the law that tidies the left side, and verify by substituting back into the untidied original.

cards.title: Advanced exponential equations extend the equating-of-indices method to…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Advanced exponential equations extend the equating-of-indices method to equations whose bases are composite (8, 9, 16, 25, 27, 125), whose unknown appears in fractional index expressions (27^(x/3) = 9^(x+1)), whose coefficients mix with powers (3^(x+2) − 3ˣ = 216), or whose values arrive as decimals (0.0625ˣ = 32). The governing conversion principle is the deepest common base: among 4, 8, 16, 32 the base 2 generates all of them integrally, so 2 is the conversion target — 8^(x+1) = (2³)^(x+1) — while a shallower choice (8) would force fractional indices for 32 (= 8^(5/3)) and invite fraction errors; for 9, 27, 81 the target is 3. The second family is magnitude comparison without computation: to compare aᵐ with bⁿ, rewrite both with the SAME exponent — aᵐ = (a^(m/d))ᵈ and bⁿ = (b^(n/d))ᵈ with d = gcd(m, n) — and compare the equal-exponent bases, since xᵈ is strictly increasing in x for x > 0: 5²⁰ = 25¹⁰ against 2⁵⁰ = 32¹⁰ settles the contest as 32 > 25. The third technique is factoring the common power: a sum or difference of like-base powers, 3^(x+2) − 3ˣ, factors as 3ˣ(3² − 1) = 8 × 3ˣ — the smaller index leaves the bracket — converting a scary difference into a product that the equating method digests. All three run on the same theory as: convert, tidy to one power (or one product containing a power), equate indices with the base's monotonicity guaranteeing uniqueness, verify in the original. The boundaries stay the same: positive bases other than 1, exact conversions only, and honest brackets ("between the 3rd and 4th hour") when a target is not an exact power.
steps: Harder equations are the same method wearing armour, and the armour comes off in a fixed order: choose the base that generates every base present integrally, convert, tidy, equate — while the comparison questions use a…

Deepest-base selection is the strategic decision of every conversion: for 8^(x+1) = 16 × 2^(2x), the bases 8, 16, 2 all live in base 2, so the equation converts wholesale: 2^(3x + 3) = 2^(4 + 2x), giving 3x + 3 = 2x + 4…
Choosing base 8 instead would meet 16 = 8^(4/3) — legal but fraction-laden; the deepest base keeps every index integral, and that is why it is chosen, not just preferred.

Fractional index expressions in x are handled by the same power-of-power law that built them: 27^(x/3) = (3³)^(x/3) = 3ˣ, so the equation 27^(x/3) = 9^(x+1) becomes 3ˣ = 3^(2x + 2), giving x = 2x + 2, x = −2; verify…

The fraction x/3 in the index is not a new species — it is an index expression like any other, and multiplication (3 × x/3) clears it. Sums and differences of like powers factor before any equating: 3^(x+2) − 3ˣ = 3ˣ(9…
Without the factoring, the left side is untidyable — the laws have no addition rule, and this factorisation is the ONLY legal move.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 4^(x+2) = 8ˣ read as 2(x + 2) = 3x "multiplying indices by the coefficients 2 and 3 without converting" — which here coincidentally gives 2x + 4 = 3x and the right answer) reveals a method that happened to work: the power-of-power…
remember: (Recall) Restate the equating-of-indices principle and the deepest-base rule, and solve 4^(x+2) = 8ˣ with verification.
(Reasoning) Solve 8^(x+1) = 32^(x−1) and explain why base 8 is an impossible conversion target while base 2 is the natural one; then generalise: given bases 4ᵏ-style composites….
(Evaluate) Solve (1/27)^(x−1) = 9^(2x), giving x as an exact fraction, and verify by simplifying both sides independently to a common value.

cards.title: Given-relations problems are index problems where the unknowns are themselves…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Given-relations problems are index problems where the unknowns are themselves INDICES tied together by an equation — aˣ = bʸ = cᶻ, or aˣ = b, bʸ = c, cᶻ = a — and the task is to derive a relation among x, y, z (prove xyz = 1, show 1/z = 1/y + 2/x, find x: y: z). Two standard tools solve the family. (1) The k-method (common parameter): set the whole chain equal to a fresh symbol k — aˣ = bʸ = cᶻ = k — and invert each relation to express the BASE as a power of k: a = k^(1/x), b = k^(1/y), c = k^(1/z). Any new equation among a, b, c (for instance abc = 1, or b² = ac) then becomes a single index equation in powers of k, and since k > 0, k ≠ 1, the indices can be equated: abc = 1 reads k^(1/x + 1/y + 1/z) = k⁰, giving 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 0. (2) Base-unification: when the bases are composite (4, 8, 9, 27 …), rewrite every relation in the deepest common base first — 4ˣ = 8ʸ = 2ᶻ becomes 2^(2x) = 2^(3y) = 2ᶻ — and read the linear relations 2x = 3y = z directly. The chapter's laws remain the engine (products add indices, brackets multiply them, positive bases give uniqueness), and the NEW skill is the modelling move: seeing that a chain of equal powers is one parameter wearing several costumes. The boundary conditions carry over — bases positive and not 1, k > 0, k ≠ 1 — and identities are verified by substitution of a numeric instance (e.g. x = 6, y = 4, z = 12 for the 4-8-2 chain) before the general proof is trusted.
steps: Given-relations problems are the chapter's algebra of costumes: one underlying quantity wears several base-index outfits, and the proofs work by unmasking it — either to one base (unification) or to one parameter (the…

Base-unification is the first reflex: a chain like 4ˣ = 8ʸ = 2ᶻ involves only base 2 in costume, so 2^(2x) = 2^(3y) = 2ᶻ — and the uniqueness of powers (each value at one index) lets you read 2x = 3y = z as three…
The method's reach is exactly the reach of the conversion table: when the bases (2, 3 together, say) have no common integral base, unification is impossible and the k-method takes over.
The k-method in action: set 2ˣ = 3ʸ = 12ᶻ = k with k > 0, k ≠ 1.
Inverting each: 2 = k^(1/x), 3 = k^(1/y), 12 = k^(1/z).
Now translate the FACT 12 = 2² × 3 into k-language: k^(1/z) = (k^(1/x))² × k^(1/y) = k^(2/x + 1/y).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., x = 3, y = 4/3 "dividing z by the base exponents in the wrong order: 12/4 and 12/9") reveals the misconception that the base's exponent divides the target value, missing that the relation is between INDICES — 2x = z comes from 4ˣ = (2²)ˣ…
remember: (Recall) State the k-method's two steps, and apply the simpler tool: given 4ˣ = 8ʸ = 2ᶻ with z = 12, find x and y, and verify both relations.
(Reasoning) In the k-method, justify the inversion a = k^(1/x) from aˣ = k, and explain why the proof then needs k > 0 and k ≠ 1 before indices may be equated.
(Evaluate) Prove the cyclic classic: if aˣ = b, bʸ = c, and cᶻ = a (a, b, c positive, ≠ 1), then xyz =….

cards.title: The synthesis of Indices and Exponents is a single routing map over the whole…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The synthesis of Indices and Exponents is a single routing map over the whole chapter's machinery, organised as two pipelines and three recognition habits. Pipeline A (simplification): convert every base to its prime stock (4, 8, 16, 32, 64 → 2; 9, 27, 81 → 3; 25, 125 → 5), run one signed index sum across all factors (brackets multiply, products add, quotients subtract — bracketed SUMS are arithmetic first), and present with positive indices (2⁻⁶ = 1/64; 2^(3/2) = 2√2). Pipeline B (equations): convert both sides to the deepest common base, tidy each side to one power, equate indices (aˣ = aʸ ⇒ x = y for a > 0, a ≠ 1), solve the linear equation, and verify in the ORIGINAL equation. Recognition habits route the question to its tool: a chain of equal powers with unknown INDICES is a k-method or unification proof (aˣ = bʸ = cᶻ = k); a comparison of aᵐ and bⁿ is a common-exponent rewrite ((a^(m/d))ᵈ versus (b^(n/d))ᵈ); a difference of like powers (3^(x+2) − 3ˣ) is a common-power factoring (3ˣ(3² − 1)); a quadratic-shaped index equation (2^(2x) − 6·2ˣ + 8 = 0) is a substitution (y = 2ˣ) with a positivity check on the roots. The chapter's three definition nodes exist by one design principle — every extension (a⁰ = 1, a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ, a^(m/n) = the nth root raised to m) was FORCED by the demand that the five laws keep holding — and the synthesis exam skill is matching each question's verbs to its pipeline: "simplify/evaluate" triggers A, "solve for x" triggers B, "prove/show" triggers the relational proofs, "which is larger" triggers the comparison rewrite.
steps: The chapter's examination promise: no new mathematics remains — only routing, speed, and presentation; the winning habit is to read the question's verb, name the pipeline, and let each line earn its mark in order.
The verb routes the question: "simplify/evaluate" means Pipeline A (convert, chain, present);
"solve for x" means Pipeline B (convert, equate, verify);
"prove that" means the relational proofs (unification for single-stock chains, the k-method for mixed ones);
"which is larger" means the common-exponent rewrite;
"find when" in a story means the growth model plus Pipeline B. Six verbs, five tools, one toolkit.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., summing −2 + 1 + 5/2 − 3/2 as 1 by dropping one of the half-terms) reveals the fraction bookkeeping slip that the written line exists to catch — in halves: −4/2 + 2/2 + 5/2 − 3/2 = 0/2; the numeric verification (2.828 ÷ 2.828)…

(Reasoning) Explain the chapter's single design principle — every extension was law-forced — by deriving a⁰ = 1, a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ, and a^(1/n) each from the law that demanded it, and….
(Evaluate) Route each item to its tool WITHOUT solving, naming the pipeline and the first move: (i) simplify (16^(−3/4) ×….

cards.title: The logarithm of a positive number x to a base a (written log_a x) is the INDEX…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The logarithm of a positive number x to a base a (written log_a x) is the INDEX to which a must be raised to produce x: a^y = x ⇔ y = log_a x, valid for a > 0, a ≠ 1, x > 0. The logarithm is not a new operation but the exponentiation a^y = x read backwards — exactly as division reads multiplication backwards and subtraction reads addition backwards; the two forms are interchangeable statements of one fact, and "write in exponential form" or "write in logarithmic form" are translation exercises. Examples in pairs: 2⁵ = 32 ⇔ log_2 32 = 5; 3⁻² = 1/9 ⇔ log_3 (1/9) = −2; 10⁴ = 10000 ⇔ log_10 10000 = 4; (1/2)⁻³ = 8 ⇔ log_(1/2) 8 = −3. Evaluating a logarithm means answering "a raised to WHAT gives x?" — log_2 64 = 6 because 2⁶ = 64; log_5 (1/125) = −3 because 5⁻³ = 1/125; log_9 27 = 3/2 because 9^(3/2) = (3²)^(3/2) = 3³ = 27. The conditions are the chapter's boundary stones: x > 0 because a positive base raised to any real index is always positive — no index produces 0 or a negative number, so log_a 0 and log_a (−5) are undefined; a > 0 keeps every power defined; a ≠ 1 because 1 to any index is 1 — log_1 7 asks "1 to the what gives 7?", which has no answer, and log_1 1 = "any index" answers nothing uniquely. Two immediate consequences ride with the definition: log_a a = 1 (a¹ = a) and log_a 1 = 0 (a⁰ = 1) — the logarithm of the base and the logarithm of unity. Because the logarithm IS an index, the whole previous chapter's machinery — the staircase for a > 1, the falling staircase for 0 < a < 1, uniqueness of values — transfers wholesale, and the index laws (aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ and friends) foreshadow the log laws of the coming nodes: multiplication of powers becomes addition of logarithms.
steps: The logarithm is the index chapter's vocabulary flipped: every power sentence "a^y = x" can be re-read as "y is the log of x to base a", and the whole skill of this node is flipping between the two readings without…
The definition is a translation table, not a formula to memorise: 2⁵ = 32 and log_2 32 = 5 are the SAME sentence — base 2, index 5, number 32.

Reading direction: in the exponential form the base sits at the bottom-left of the power; in the log form the base is the subscript of "log" and the number sits beside it. Flipping drills: 3⁴ = 81 becomes log_3 81 = 4…

Evaluation is common-base rewriting in disguise: log_9 27 asks "9 to the what gives 27?" — write both as powers of 3: 9 = 3², 27 = 3³, so the question becomes (3²)^y = 3³, i.e. 3^(2y) = 3³, giving y = 3/2.
Every exact log evaluation is Pipeline B from the indices chapter wearing log notation; the fraction answers (3/2, −5/3) are ordinary index answers.

The conditions are answerable "why" questions, each inherited from the indices chapter: x > 0 because a positive base never produces a non-positive power (the staircase never touches the ground); a ≠ 1 because the…

cards.title: The laws of logarithms are three theorems…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The laws of logarithms are three theorems, each proved from the definition a^y = x, that describe how logarithms interact with multiplication, division and powers. For a legal base (a > 0, a ≠ 1) and positive numbers x, y: the product law states log_a (xy) = log_a x + log_a y — the log of a product is the SUM of the logs; the quotient law states log_a (x/y) = log_a x − log_a y — the log of a quotient is the DIFFERENCE of the logs; the power law states log_a (xⁿ) = n log_a x for any real n — a power inside the log comes out as a coefficient. Each law is an equality of two readings of one index fact: if log_a x = m then x = aᵐ, and if log_a y = n then y = aⁿ; multiplying gives xy = aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ (the first index law), and reading that sentence back through the flip yields the product law; dividing yields aᵐ⁻ⁿ and the quotient law; raising x to the n-th power yields (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ and the power law. The proofs are thus two-line translations of the index laws — this is why the laws are theorems with proofs, not definitions to accept on trust, and CISCE expects the proof of each law to be reproducible. Three structural points ride with the statements: all logarithms in one expression must share ONE base — mixing log_2 and log_3 inside a single application of a law is illegal; the inputs x, y must be positive so the logs exist at all; and each law generates corollaries — log_a (1/x) = log_a 1 − log_a x = 0 − log_a x = −log_a x (the reciprocal rule), log_a (x/y) may also be read as log_a x + log_a (1/y), and the power law with a fractional n handles roots: log_a √x = (1/2) log_a x. The laws do NOT say anything about log_a (x + y) — no law exists for the log of a sum — and they do not let logs of different bases mix.
steps: The three laws of logarithms are the index laws read through the logarithm's flip, and each proof is the same two-line move: write every log as an index sentence, combine with the matching index law, and read the result…
The product law proof, slowly: let log_a x = m; by the definition this MEANS x = aᵐ.
Let log_a y = n; this means y = aⁿ.
Multiply the two index sentences: xy = aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ — that is exactly the first index law from the indices chapter.

Now read xy = aᵐ⁺ⁿ back through the flip: "the log of xy to base a is m + n", i.e. log_a (xy) = m + n = log_a x + log_a y. Nothing was assumed except the definition and aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; the law is a theorem, and…

The quotient law uses the same scaffold with division: x = aᵐ, y = aⁿ, so x/y = aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ, and reading back gives log_a (x/y) = m − n = log_a x − log_a y. The subtraction on the log side is the subtraction of…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., stating the product law as log_a (xy) = log_a x × log_a y "multiplying the logs because the numbers multiply") reveals the misconception that the law preserves the outer operation, missing that the whole point of the law is the operation…
remember: (Recall) State the three laws of logarithms with all conditions, and verify the product law numerically using log_2 8, log_2 16 and their product.
(Reasoning) Prove the quotient law from the definition in full, and explain precisely why the proof fails if x = 0 or if one log is taken to a different base.
(Evaluate) Evaluate log_2 10 + log_2 12.8 − log_2 0.5 in one line using the laws, and verify the final value by exponentiating.

cards.title: Expansion is the rewriting of a single logarithm of a product…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Expansion is the rewriting of a single logarithm of a product, quotient or power into a sum and difference of simpler logarithms, by reading the three laws right-to-left: log_a (√x · y³/z²) = (1/2) log_a x + 3 log_a y − 2 log_a z. Condensation is the reverse move — collecting a sum of same-base logarithms, with their coefficients folded back by the power law, into ONE logarithm: 2 log_a x + 3 log_a y − log_a z = log_a (x²y³/z). Evaluation with given values uses decomposition: any positive number whose prime factors are known can have its logarithm computed from a small stock of given values — if log_10 2 = 0.3010 and log_10 3 = 0.4771, then log_10 72 = log_10 (2³ × 3²) = 3(0.3010) + 2(0.4771) = 1.8572, because every law used is an equality proved in the previous node. Both directions are LEGAL only under the standing conditions: every input positive, every logarithm to the SAME base, coefficients folded by the power law (a coefficient n multiplies the LOG, never the input), and no law ever splits a sum inside the log. Alongside the two directions sits the cancellation identity: a^(log_a x) = x for all legal a and positive x — the base and the log-operation undo each other, since log_a x = t means exactly x = aᵗ — together with its twin log_a (aᵏ) = k. Expansion and condensation are exact, value-preserving rewritings: the expression before and after is the SAME number, which is what makes them useful for evaluation and for solving equations later in the chapter.
steps: Expansion and condensation are the three laws run forwards and backwards, and evaluation is condensation aimed at a number — one toolkit, three directions, and every direction preserves the value exactly.

The expansion algorithm is a fixed order: first bring every exponent down (power law — coefficients for powers AND fractional coefficients for roots), then split the numerator at multiplications (product law), then…

Example, this order: log_a (x³√y/z²) → 3 log_a x + log_a √y − 2 log_a z → 3 log_a x + (1/2) log_a y − 2 log_a z. Working root-to-coefficient FIRST keeps roots from being forgotten at the end — the most common lost mark…

Condensation runs the opposite order: fold every coefficient into a power (2 log_a x becomes log_a x²), then collect the numerator logs by addition and the subtracted logs into one quotient: 2 log_a x + 3 log_a y −…
Finish with coefficient 1 — a condensed answer still wearing a coefficient is half-condensed.

Evaluation with given values is decomposition plus condensation: to get log_10 720, factor 720 = 72 × 10 = 2³ × 3² × 10, so log_10 720 = 3 log_10 2 + 2 log_10 3 + log_10 10 = 3(0.3010) + 2(0.4771) + 1 = 0.9030 + 0.9542…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., expanding (b) as log_a √x + log_a y³ = log_a x + 3 log_a y "dropping the root silently") reveals the lost-fraction error, missing that √x is x^(1/2) and the power law hands the 1/2 to the COEFFICIENT; a quick numeric referee — a = 4, x =…
remember: (Recall) Expand fully: (a) log_a (x²y/z); (b) log_a (√x · y³); (c) log_10 (100x/y²). State which law is used at each step.
(Reasoning) Explain why expansion and condensation are exact rewritings rather than approximations, and why the rewriting log_a (x + y) = log_a x + log_a y — though it LOOKS like….
(Evaluate) Given log_10 2 = 0.3010 and log_10 3 = 0.4771, evaluate log_10 1.5, and verify your answer by bracketing between two known logs.

cards.title: The common logarithm is the logarithm to base 10…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The common logarithm is the logarithm to base 10, written log N with no subscript. Every positive number N has a unique split in standard form N = p × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ p < 10 and n an integer, and taking logs gives log N = n + log p — an integer part plus a fractional part. The integer n is the characteristic: it records the SIZE (the power of ten), equals (digits − 1) for numbers ≥ 1, and is negative for numbers between 0 and 1 (0.045 = 4.5 × 10⁻² has characteristic −2). The fractional part log p is the mantissa: it records only the significant DIGITS, is always kept positive (0 ≤ mantissa < 1), and is the part logarithm tables supply, since tables list only 1 to 10. When the characteristic is negative it is written in bar notation — a bar over the integer — because the mantissa must stay positive: log 0.045 = log (4.5 × 10⁻²) = −2 + 0.6532, written 2̄.6532, and this is NOT the number −2.6532 (it is −1.3468). Three working consequences: (i) multiplying by a power of 10 shifts only the characteristic — log 720 = 2.8572 and log 72000 = 4.8572 share the mantissa.8572; (ii) all numbers with the same significant digits share one mantissa — 3, 30, 300, 0.3, 0.003 all carry.4771; (iii) the digit-count rule: if log N has characteristic n, then N has n + 1 digits (log 720 = 2.8572 → characteristic 2 → 3 digits ✓). The characteristic-mantissa split is exactly the place-value insight that base 10 earns: the power of ten and the digit-string separate cleanly, and every computation with tables in the next node is this split being exploited.
steps: The common logarithm is the logarithm dressed for our place-value system, and its whole anatomy is one split: standard form N = p × 10ⁿ turns log N into characteristic n (the size, an integer) plus mantissa log p (the…
The split is a computation, not a slogan.
Take 720: standard form 7.2 × 10², so log 720 = 2 + log 7.2.
The stock of the last node supplies log 7.2 = log (72/10) = log (2³ × 3²) − 1 = (0.9030 + 0.9542) − 1 = 0.8572, so log 720 = 2.8572 — characteristic 2 (3-digit number: 3 − 1 = 2), mantissa.8572.
The characteristic came from COUNTING tens; the mantissa came from the DIGITS 7-2 only.
Numbers below 1 are where the design shows.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., calling.8572 the characteristic and 2 the mantissa "the bigger part leads") reveals role-confusion, missing that the characteristic is by definition the INTEGER part n of log N = n + mantissa and the mantissa the fractional part; the…

(Reasoning) Explain why mantissas are always kept positive (and negative characteristics written as bars), and what would go wrong with a table-based system if mantissas were….
(Evaluate) Write log 0.045 in bar notation by decomposing 0.045 in standard form, computing the mantissa from log 2 = 0.3010 and log 3 = 0.4771, and give the value as an ordinary….

cards.title: The logarithm table (four-figure) tabulates mantissas…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The logarithm table (four-figure) tabulates mantissas: rows labelled by the first two significant digits (10–99), columns by the third digit (0–9), and mean-difference columns (1–9) that append the correction for a fourth digit. Reading log 4.2's mantissa is a row 42 lookup:.6232; a number like 4.267 would take the row-42 column-6 entry plus the mean difference for 7. The characteristic is NEVER tabulated — it comes from the standard form (07_004): log 0.42 = 1̄.6232, log 42 = 1.6232, log 4200 = 3.6232 all share the one tabulated fraction. The antilogarithm inverts the log: if log N = x then N = antilog x; the antilog table is read the reverse way — locate the mantissa's first two decimals as a row, the third as a column, mean differences for the fourth — and returns the digit-string, to which the characteristic attaches the decimal point: antilog 0.6232 = 4.2, so antilog 1̄.6232 = 0.42 and antilog 1.6232 = 42.0... i.e. 42. The log-method computation of an expression built from multiplications, divisions, powers and roots runs: (i) take the log of the whole expression (laws of 07_002/07_003); (ii) evaluate that single log using tables for mantissas and bar arithmetic for characteristics; (iii) antilog the result back to the answer. In this course's stock presentation the mantissas come from derivable values (log 2 = 0.3010, log 3 = 0.4771, log 5 = 0.6990, log 7 = 0.8451) exactly as tables would supply them, so every working below is verifiable to four figures. Bar arithmetic rules carry over: multiply/divide the bar part and the fraction part separately, keeping the fraction positive and less than 1, and when a characteristic must be divided (roots), rewrite first so it is divisible — 3̄.9084 = −2.0916 = (−4 + 1.9084), which halves to 2̄.9542.
steps: Table-based computation is the characteristic-mantissa split turned into an engine: tables hold nothing but mantissas, you hold the characteristics, and the laws of 07_002 reduce every product-quotient-power-root…
The pipeline for (7.2 × 3.5)/0.42: first LOG the whole expression: log answer = log 7.2 + log 3.5 − log 0.42.
Antilog:.7781 is the mantissa of 6 (log 6 = 0.7781), characteristic 1 → answer 60.
Direct check: 7.2 × 3.5 = 25.2, and 25.2/0.42 = 60 ✓ — the whole product-quotient collapsed to two additions and one subtraction.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., giving log 4200's characteristic as 4 "four digits, characteristic four") reveals the off-by-one — characteristic = digits − 1; the standard form 4.2 × 10³ shows the 3 directly, and 10³ ≤ 4200 < 10⁴ pins the log between 3 and 4.
remember: (Recall) Describe the layout of a four-figure logarithm table and the role of mean….
(Reasoning) Explain why a log table can be finite yet serve every positive number, and why an antilog table also needs only mantissa-sized entries even though answers can be huge….
(Evaluate) Evaluate (0.3)³ by the log method: take the log, multiply in bar notation with the carry shown, antilog back, and verify directly.

cards.title: This node extends the laws of logarithms
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: This node extends the laws of logarithms (product, quotient, power) to solve exponential equations where the unknown appears in the exponent, and it introduces three standard logarithmic scales used across sciences: pH (chemistry), decibel level (physics), and Richter magnitude (earth science). The core mathematical principle is that any exponential equation a^x = b (with a>0, a≠1, b>0) can be rewritten as x = _a b, and the change-of-base formula _a b = ( _c b)/( _c a) allows evaluation using common (base 10) or natural (base e) logarithms available on calculators. Real-world scales are defined as: pH = - _10[H^+] where [H^+] is hydrogen ion concentration in mol/L; dB = 10 _10(I/I_0) where I is sound intensity in W/m² and I_0 = 10^-12 W/m² is the reference threshold; M = _10(A/A_0) where A is seismic wave amplitude and A_0 is a reference amplitude. These scales compress multiplicative ranges (e.g., intensity ratios of 10^12) into additive intervals (0–120 dB), making comparison intuitive. The node connects prior knowledge of logarithmic–exponential conversion (node 002) and logarithmic laws (node 003) to practical problem-solving, emphasizing that the same algebraic structure underlies diverse phenomena.
steps: Logarithms transform difficult exponential problems into simpler linear ones, and they provide the mathematical backbone for everyday scales like pH, decibels, and earthquake magnitude.
Here is why: first, any exponential equation a^x = b becomes x = _a b, turning an unknown exponent into a solvable logarithm.
Second, the change-of-base formula lets us compute _a b using base-10 or base-e logarithms on a standard calculator.
Third, the product, quotient, and power laws allow us to combine or break apart logarithmic terms before evaluation, reducing arithmetic errors.

Fourth, real-world logarithmic scales (pH, dB, Richter) are defined exactly by these logarithmic forms, so a one-unit increase always represents a tenfold (pH, Richter) or tenfold-power (dB) change in the underlying…
Fifth, interpreting these scales requires understanding that they are logarithmic, not linear — a common trap in exams.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 5^2 = 32) reveals the misconception that the base and exponent are swapped — confusing the logarithmic notation _base argument = exponent with exponent^base = argument.
remember: Write the exponential form of _2 32 = 5.
If _10 x = 2.3, estimate x without a calculator.
A student claims that _5 125 = 3 because 5 × 3 = 15. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: A logarithmic equation has the unknown inside a logarithm (log_10 x + log_10
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A logarithmic equation has the unknown inside a logarithm (log_10 x + log_10 (x + 3) = 1); an exponential equation has it in the exponent (5^x = 3^(x + 2)). The solution machinery is the chapter in reverse. For log equations: condense all log terms of one base into a single logarithm (product/quotient/power laws), then use the one-to-one property — log_a A = log_a B implies A = B, because the base-a staircase is strictly increasing, so equal heights mean equal inputs — to drop the logs and solve the resulting algebraic equation; finally test every candidate against the ORIGINAL domains (every log's input positive; every base a > 0, a ≠ 1), rejecting extraneous roots produced by the algebra. For exponential equations with a common base, equate exponents (2^m = 2^n ⇒ m = n, same monotonicity); with different bases, take log_10 of both sides and use the power law to bring the unknown exponent down as a coefficient (5^x = 3^(x+2) becomes x log 5 = (x + 2) log 3); equations like 4^x − 6 · 2^x + 8 = 0 are disguised quadratics — substitute y = 2^x, solve for y, then convert back with x = log_2 y. Two structural facts govern everything: the condensation step (log A + log B = log AB) is an equality only for A, B > 0, which is precisely why the domain check must consult the ORIGINAL equation's inputs, not the condensed one's; and admissibility of a log's BASE (positive, ≠ 1) applies when the unknown sits in the base seat (log_x 49 = 2 gives x = 7, rejecting x = −7 if it appears).
steps: Equation-solving is the chapter run backwards: the laws condense the equation to one log, the one-to-one property strips the log, and ordinary algebra finishes — with the domain check as the gatekeeper that the…
The canonical log equation, full pipeline: log_10 x + log_10 (x + 3) = 1.
Condense: log_10 (x(x + 3)) = 1.
Strip: the one-to-one property says the input that logs to 1 is 10 itself (10¹ = 10), so x² + 3x = 10, i.e. x² + 3x − 10 = 0, giving (x + 5)(x − 2) = 0 — candidates x = 2 and x = −5.
Domain check against the ORIGINAL: log_10 x needs x > 0, so −5 dies before it is ever substituted; the solution is x = 2.
Verify: log 2 + log 5 = log 10 = 1 ✓.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., (b) answered as ±5 "the quadratic's two roots") reveals treating the conversion as the finish line, missing that a^y = x ⇔ y = log_a x holds only under a > 0, a ≠ 1, x > 0 — the conditions are part of the definition, not a post-solve…
remember: (Recall) Solve: (a) log_3 x = 4; (b) log_x 25 = 2; (c) log_5 (1/x) = −1. State the admissibility check in each.
(Reasoning) State the one-to-one property for logarithms and prove it from the staircase….

cards.title: A synthesis node integrates every skill of the Logarithms chapter into…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A synthesis node integrates every skill of the Logarithms chapter into exam-ready problem solving. The chapter built five connected layers. First, the definition: log_a x = y is equivalent to a^y = x, valid for a > 0, a ≠ 1, x > 0. Second, the three laws — product law log_a(xy) = log_a x + log_a y, quotient law log_a(x/y) = log_a x − log_a y, power law log_a(x^n) = n log_a x — which let any complicated product be expanded into sums and differences or condensed back into one logarithm. Third, the computational machinery of common logarithms: every positive number N written in standard form N = p × 10^n (1 ≤ p < 10) gives log N = n + log p, where the integer n is the characteristic (written with a bar, e.g. 2̄, when negative) and log p read from four-figure tables is the mantissa; the final answer is recovered with the antilog table. Fourth, applications: exponential growth or decay models N = N₀ × g^t, solved by taking logs, using supplied values such as log 2 = 0.3010. Fifth, logarithmic and exponential equations, solved by condensing to a single log and stripping it with the one-to-one property, always checking that solutions keep every argument positive. Synthesis means selecting and sequencing these layers correctly under exam conditions: recognising which law to apply first, tracking characteristics through multiplication and division, rejecting invalid roots, and stating answers to the precision the marking scheme expects.
steps: Every full Logarithms exam question is the same five-move sequence: decide the laws, expand, compute logs, combine characteristics and mantissas, and finish with antilog or algebra.
Why does this sequence work?

Because the three laws convert multiplication and division of awkward decimals into addition and subtraction of small table-friendly numbers; because the characteristic tracks the decimal point so the mantissa tables…

In (8.36)² × √0.0074 ÷ 248.5, name the pieces: a square, a square root, a division.
Log of the whole thing = 2 log 8.36 + ½ log 0.0074 − log 248.5.
