Explain why magnetic force is classified as a non‑contact force even though a magnet must be brought close to a paperclip to attract it.

cards.title: The centimetre‑gram‑second (cgs) system and the Système International d’Unités…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The centimetre‑gram‑second (cgs) system and the Système International d’Unités (SI) system are two metric systems used to express physical quantities. In the cgs system the base units are: length – centimetre (cm, symbol l), mass – gram (g, symbol m), time – second (s, symbol t). In the SI system the base units are: length – metre (m, symbol L), mass – kilogram (kg, symbol M), time – second (s, symbol T). All other units are derived from these bases. For example, force is mass × acceleration. In cgs the unit of force is the dyne (dyn), where 1 dyn = 1 g·cm s⁻². In SI the unit of force is the newton (N), where 1 N = 1 kg·m s⁻². Because 1 kg = 10³ g and 1 m = 10² cm, the conversion is 1 N = 10⁵ dyn. Similarly, energy (work) is force × distance: the cgs unit is the erg (erg = 1 dyn·cm = 1 g·cm² s⁻²) and the SI unit is the joule (J = 1 N·m = 1 kg·m² s⁻²), giving 1 J = 10⁷ erg. Pressure is force per area: cgs uses barye (Ba = 1 dyn·cm⁻²) and SI uses pascal (Pa = 1 N·m⁻²), with 1 Pa = 10 Ba. Thus every derived unit in one system relates to the other by a power of ten, determined solely by the differences in the base units.
steps: The SI system uses metre, kilogram, second as base units, while the cgs system uses centimetre, gram, second, and all derived units are related by powers of ten. First, both systems share the same second for time, so…

Second, the length base differs by a factor of 10²: 1 m = 100 cm. Therefore any quantity that contains length to the power n acquires a factor (10²)ⁿ when switching from cgs to SI. Third, the mass base differs by a…

Combining these, a derived unit that depends on massᵐ · lengthⁿ · timeᵖ changes by (10³)ᵐ · (10²)ⁿ · (1)ᵖ = 10^(3m+2n) when going from cgs to SI. Consider force: mass¹·length¹·time⁻² → m = 1, n = 1 → factor…
In cgs this is 2 N × 10⁵ dyn/N = 2 × 10⁵ dyn. If you measure the book’s thickness as 2 cm, its volume in cgs is length³ → (2 cm)³ = 8 cm³; converting to SI gives 8 cm³ × (10⁻² m/cm)³ = 8 × 10⁻⁶ m³.

Thus, once you know how each base unit scales, you can convert any derived quantity by counting the powers of mass and length and applying the appropriate power of ten. This method avoids memorising countless conversion…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “dyne”) reveals the misconception that the cgs unit also serves as the SI unit, confusing the two systems’ parallel structures.
remember: What is the SI unit of force.
Explain why the cgs unit of force is called a dyne.
Evaluate the statement: “Because 1 kg equals 1000 g, 1 newton must equal 1000 dyne.”.

cards.title: Newton’s first law of motion, also known as the law of inertia…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Newton’s first law of motion, also known as the law of inertia, states that a body remains at rest or continues to move with constant velocity in a straight line unless acted upon by a net external force. Inertia is the intrinsic property of matter that quantifies this resistance to change in motion; it is measured by the mass of the body. The greater the mass, the greater the inertia, and the larger the force required to produce a given acceleration. The law establishes the concept of an inertial frame of reference — a frame in which a body not subjected to forces moves uniformly. It connects directly with the earlier nodes: contact forces (push, pull, friction) and non‑contact forces (gravity, magnetism) are the agents that can change a body’s state of motion, and the SI unit of force, the newton (N), is defined from the second law but is already introduced in the units node. The first law does not provide a quantitative formula; it defines the condition of zero net force (∑F = 0) leading to zero acceleration (a = 0). It also implies that if a body is observed to accelerate, a net force must be present, setting the stage for Newton’s second law.
steps: Newton’s first law states that a body remains at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by a net external force.
Here is why: (1) Inertia is not a force but a property of mass; it explains why a massive truck needs a larger push than a bicycle to start moving.
(2) When the net force on a body is zero, its acceleration is zero, so its velocity — both magnitude and direction — stays constant.
(3) An inertial frame is any frame moving at constant velocity; in such frames the first law holds without fictitious forces.
Consider a book lying on a classroom desk.
The book experiences its weight downward and the normal reaction upward; these forces balance, giving zero net force.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “An object in motion stays in motion forever”) reveals the misconception that the law ignores the need for a net force to change motion and omits the condition of zero net force.
remember: State Newton’s first law of motion.
A book lies on a horizontal table. Explain why it does not move unless pushed.
A student says, “Inertia is a force that keeps objects moving.” Evaluate this statement.

cards.title: Newton’s second law of motion quantifies how a net external force changes the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Newton’s second law of motion quantifies how a net external force changes the motion of a body. It states that the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied net force and occurs in the direction of that force. For a body of constant mass m, momentum p = mv, so the law reduces to F = ma, where F is the net force (vector, SI unit newton, N), m is the mass (scalar, kilogram, kg) and a is the acceleration (vector, metre per second squared, m s⁻²). The law links three concepts from earlier nodes: force (contact or non‑contact), mass (a measure of inertia from Newton’s first law), and acceleration (change in velocity). In the cgs system the corresponding units are dyne for force, gram for mass and cm s⁻² for acceleration (1 N = 10⁵ dyne). The law also provides the operational definition of the newton: one newton is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m s⁻².
steps: Newton’s second law tells us that the acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass.
Here is why: the law originates from the definition of momentum p = mv. A force changes momentum; the faster the momentum changes, the larger the force.

For everyday objects whose mass stays constant, the change in momentum per second is m Δv/Δt = ma. Therefore, if you double the push on a 2 kg block, its acceleration doubles; if you keep the push the same but double…
Consider a cricket ball (mass ≈ 0.16 kg) bowled at 30 m s⁻¹ and stopped in 0.02 s by a wicket‑keeper’s gloves.
The change in velocity is –30 m s⁻¹, so acceleration = –1500 m s⁻².
The average force exerted by the gloves is F = ma = 0.16 × (–1500) = –240 N (the negative sign shows the force opposes the motion).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “F = mv”) reveals the misconception that force equals momentum rather than the rate of change of momentum.
remember: State the mathematical form of Newton’s second law for a body of constant mass and name the SI unit of each quantity.
A 5 kg block is pulled across a horizontal frictionless surface by a horizontal force of 20 N. What is its….
Two forces, 30 N east and 40 N north, act simultaneously on a 10 kg object initially at rest. Determine the magnitude and direction of its acceleration.

cards.title: Momentum is the quantity of motion of a body…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Momentum is the quantity of motion of a body, defined as the product of its mass and its velocity: p = mv. It is a vector — its direction is the direction of the body's velocity, and its sign follows the axis sentence exactly as velocity's does (a 2 kg body moving at 5 m s⁻¹ east has momentum 10 kg m s⁻¹ east; the same body moving 5 m s⁻¹ west on an east-positive axis has p = −10 kg m s⁻¹). Units: SI — kg m s⁻¹; CGS — g cm s⁻¹; the bridge is the same powers-of-ten bookkeeping as always (1 kg m s⁻¹ = 10³ g × 10² cm s⁻¹ = 10⁵ g cm s⁻¹, mirroring the newton–dyne bridge of because momentum's unit is mass × velocity just as force's is mass × acceleration). Momentum measures "how much motion" in a way VELOCITY alone cannot: a loaded truck at 2 m s⁻¹ and a cricket ball at 40 m s⁻¹ — the truck's p (say 4000 kg × 2 = 8000 kg m s⁻¹) dwarfs the ball's (0.16 × 40 = 6.4), even though the ball is twenty times faster; the number that predicts what each will do to a fence is the momentum, not the speed. The second law of motion in its full form is ABOUT this quantity: the rate of change of momentum is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of the force — in symbols, F = Δp/t = (mv − mu)/t, which for constant mass collapses to F = m(v − u)/t = ma: the F = ma used all through the previous node is the constant-mass face of the momentum law, and this node works with the general face. Δp = mv − mu is the change of momentum — final minus initial, signs honest — so a body brought to rest has Δp = 0 − mu = −mu (the minus means the momentum was REMOVED), and a reversing body (u = +10, v = −14) has Δp = m(−14 − 10) = −24m, larger in magnitude than either stopping or doubling. The rate form's most practical reading: for a GIVEN change of momentum, the force shrinks in proportion as the contact time grows (F = Δp/t, t in the denominator) — the single equation behind catching a ball with drawn-back hands, landing with bent knees, and every crash-cushion ever built. Momentum's deep career — its conservation when no net external force acts — is a Class 10 continuation; this node computes p, Δp and the forces they imply.
steps: Momentum is the account-book of motion — every force is a transaction that adds or removes p = mv at the rate F = Δp/t — and mastering this node means reading that ledger in both directions: from masses and velocities…
Argument one: momentum is what velocity alone refuses to tell you — the product is the physics.
The mosquito and the truck at the same speed differ in consequence by their masses; the bullet and the thrown stone differ by their speeds; only the PRODUCT ranks them on one scale.

The definition p = mv inherits direction from velocity, so momentum bookkeeping is Chapter 2's sign discipline re-run: east-positive, a 0.5 kg ball at 8 m s⁻¹ east is +4 kg m s⁻¹; the same ball 8 m s⁻¹ west is −4; and a…

This is where reversal cases earn their reputation: the change across a turnaround is u + |v| in magnitude (the velocity passed through zero and kept going), the largest Δp any given speeds can produce.
Students who subtract magnitudes blindly (8 − 8 = 0) turn the hardest kick in the paper into no change at all — the sign is not decoration; it is the entire physics of the turnaround.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "momentum is a scalar because it is mass times speed", "the unit of momentum is the newton", or stating the law as "force = momentum") reveals three separable faults: the scalar/speed slip — mass times VELOCITY with the mass's positive…
remember: Recall: define momentum, state its vector or scalar nature with the reason, write its SI and CGS units with their exact relation, and state the second law in its momentum form….
Reasoning: A 20 g bullet fired at 400 m s⁻¹ horizontally embeds in a wooden block of mass 3 kg hanging at….
Analyse: A 0.5 kg ball travels horizontally at 8 m s⁻¹….

cards.title: Newton’s third law states that for every action force there is an equal and…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Newton’s third law states that for every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force. If body A exerts a force F_AB on body B, then body B simultaneously exerts a force F_BA on body A such that F_AB = –F_BA. The two forces are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and act on different bodies; therefore they never cancel each other. This law applies to all contact forces (e.g., normal reaction, friction) and non‑contact forces (e.g., gravitational attraction, electrostatic force). It is the foundation for understanding momentum conservation in isolated systems, because the internal action‑reaction pairs sum to zero net force. The law does not imply that the bodies experience the same acceleration — acceleration depends on each body’s mass (Newton’s second law). In the CISCE curriculum, the third law is introduced after momentum (node) to show how force pairs explain changes in momentum during collisions and propulsion.
steps: Newton’s third law tells us that forces always come in equal‑and‑opposite pairs acting on two different objects.
Here is why: when you push a desk, your hand exerts a force on the desk; the desk simultaneously exerts a force of the same size back on your hand.

The two forces are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and act on different bodies — your hand and the desk — so they never cancel each other out. First, recognise that the law applies to every interaction…
Second, the pair is always of the same type: if the action is gravitational, the reaction is also gravitational.
Third, the accelerations produced are generally different because the masses differ (a = F/m).

Fourth, the law explains everyday phenomena: a swimmer pushes water backward (action) and water pushes the swimmer forward (reaction); a rocket expels hot gases downward and the gases push the rocket upward.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “action and reaction cancel so nothing moves”) reveals the misconception that the two forces act on the same object, confusing Newton’s third law with equilibrium of forces on a single body.
remember: State Newton’s third law in your own words.
Why do the action and reaction forces not cancel each other to produce zero net force on a system.
Evaluate the statement: “A rocket moves forward because the exhaust gases push against the ground.”.

cards.title: Gravitation is a universal non‑contact force of attraction that exists between…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Gravitation is a universal non‑contact force of attraction that exists between any two particles of matter. Newton’s law of universal gravitation states that every point mass attracts every other point mass with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres. Mathematically, F = G m₁ m₂ / r², where F is the gravitational force (newton, N), m₁ and m₂ are the masses (kilogram, kg), r is the centre‑to‑centre separation (metre, m), and G is the universal gravitational constant (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²·kg⁻²). The force acts along the line joining the centres and is always attractive; it obeys Newton’s third law, so the two bodies experience equal and opposite forces. Because G is extremely small, gravitational force is negligible for everyday laboratory masses but becomes dominant for astronomical bodies. The weight of an object on Earth (W = mg) is the gravitational force exerted by the Earth: mg = G Mₑ m / Rₑ², giving the acceleration due to gravity g = G Mₑ / Rₑ². This node introduces the law, the constant G, its SI unit, and the qualitative idea that gravitation governs planetary motion, tides, and the weight we feel. It does not derive g’s variation with altitude or latitude, nor does it cover orbital mechanics or Kepler’s laws, which are treated in later chapters.
steps: Every object in the universe pulls every other object with a force that depends only on their masses and the distance between them.
Here is why: first, gravitation is a non‑contact force — it acts without any medium, unlike friction or tension.

Second, Newton discovered that the magnitude of this pull is directly proportional to the product of the two masses and inversely proportional to the square of the centre‑to‑centre distance; doubling the distance…

Third, the proportionality constant G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²·kg⁻² is extremely small, so the force between everyday objects (e.g., two 1 kg spheres 1 m apart) is only about 6.7 × 10⁻¹¹ N — too tiny to feel.

Fourth, when one mass is the Earth (Mₑ ≈ 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg) and the other is a person (m = 60 kg) at the surface (Rₑ ≈ 6.4 × 10⁶ m), the same formula gives a force of roughly 586 N, which we experience as weight.
Fifth, the force always acts along the line joining the centres and is mutually attractive, satisfying Newton’s third law. Consider a mango falling from a tree in a backyard in Kerala.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “F = G m₁ m₂ / r”) reveals the misconception that the force falls off linearly with distance instead of as an inverse square.

cards.title: Fluids are substances that continuously deform under shear stress…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Fluids are substances that continuously deform under shear stress; they include liquids and gases. The chapter introduces five interlinked concepts. First, pressure in a fluid increases linearly with depth because the weight of the fluid column above any point adds to the force per unit area (p = hρg). Second, buoyancy is the net upward force exerted by a fluid on an immersed object, equal to the weight of the displaced fluid. Third, Archimedes’ principle formalises this: the buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced. Fourth, flotation occurs when the buoyant force balances the object’s weight; the condition for floating is that the object’s average density is less than or equal to the fluid’s density. Fifth, density (ρ = m/V) and relative density (RD = ρ_substance/ρ_water at 4 °C) provide a way to compare how compact matter is without units. Together these ideas explain everyday phenomena — from why a hydrometer sinks to a certain level in milk to why submarines adjust ballast tanks to dive or surface.
steps: The chapter shows that fluids exert pressure that grows with depth, and this pressure creates an upward buoyant force that can balance weight.
Here is why: pressure at a depth h in a fluid of density ρ is p = hρg, so deeper points feel larger force per area.
Consider a cylindrical column of water 1 m high and 1 cm² cross‑section; its weight is ρVg = (1000 kg m⁻³)(1 × 10⁻⁶ m³)(9.8 m s⁻²) ≈ 0.0098 N, giving a pressure of 98 Pa at the bottom.
This pressure acts in all directions, pushing up on any submerged surface.
When an object is placed in the fluid, the pressure on its lower surface is greater than on its upper surface, producing a net upward force — the buoyant force.
Archimedes discovered that this force exactly equals the weight of the fluid displaced by the object.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “pressure is measured in newtons”) reveals the misconception that pressure and force are the same quantity, confusing a scalar intensity with a vector force.
remember: What is the SI unit of pressure and how is it defined in terms of force and area.
A solid cube of side 5 cm and mass 250 g is fully immersed in water (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³). Will it float or sink? Justify using densities.
Evaluate the statement: “The buoyant force on an object depends on the depth at which it is submerged.”.

cards.title: Pressure at a depth h in a fluid is the sum of the atmospheric pressure at the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Pressure at a depth h in a fluid is the sum of the atmospheric pressure at the free surface (P₀) and the pressure due to the fluid column above that point. The fluid pressure contribution equals the weight of a column of fluid of cross‑sectional area A and height h divided by A, giving ρgh, where ρ is the fluid density and g is the acceleration due to gravity. Thus the absolute pressure is P = P₀ + ρgh. This linear relationship holds for incompressible fluids (liquids) under constant g. The gauge pressure (pressure above atmospheric) is ρgh. The concept links force, area, density, and gravity, and underpins later topics such as buoyancy and Archimedes’ principle.
steps: Pressure in a fluid increases linearly with depth because the weight of the fluid above adds to the atmospheric pressure at the surface.
Here is why: 1.
Atmospheric pressure acts on the free surface — the air column above the liquid exerts P₀ (≈ 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa). 2.

A fluid element at depth h supports the weight of the column above it — consider a vertical cylinder of cross‑section A extending from the surface to depth h. The fluid in that cylinder has mass m = ρAh.
Its weight mg = ρAhg acts downward on the bottom face. 3.
Force balance on the bottom face — the upward force from the fluid below must balance the downward forces: atmospheric force P₀A plus weight ρAhg.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 4.0 × 10³ Pa) reveals the misconception that the density value can be used directly without multiplying by g and h, or that the student forgot to multiply by depth.
remember: What is the gauge pressure at a depth of 5 m in a liquid of density 800 kg m⁻³? (Take g = 10 m s⁻².).
A student argues that pressure at the bottom of a narrow tube filled with water is less than at the bottom of a wide bucket with the same water depth. Evaluate this claim.
If atmospheric pressure is 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa, what is the absolute pressure at 12 m depth in seawater (ρ = 1025 kg m⁻³, g = 9.8 m s⁻²).

cards.title: Buoyancy is the net upward force exerted by a fluid on any object that is…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Buoyancy is the net upward force exerted by a fluid on any object that is partially or completely immersed in it. The force originates from the pressure gradient that exists in a fluid at rest: pressure increases linearly with depth according to p = p_0 + ρ_f g h. Consequently, the pressure acting on the lower surface of an immersed body is greater than the pressure on its upper surface. The resultant of these distributed pressure forces is a single upward force called the buoyant force (F_b). Its magnitude equals the weight of the fluid displaced by the volume of the object that lies below the free surface, i.e. F_b = ρ_f V_disp g, where ρ_f is the fluid density, V_disp the displaced volume, and g the acceleration due to gravity. Buoyancy explains why objects appear lighter in water and provides the basis for Archimedes’ principle, floatation criteria, and the concept of relative density. It links directly to the pressure‑depth relationship covered earlier and to the density concepts that follow.
steps: The buoyant force on an immersed object is the direct result of fluid pressure increasing with depth, producing a larger upward push on the bottom than the downward push on the top. Here is why: (1) In a static fluid…
(3) The net vertical force is the pressure difference times the horizontal cross‑sectional area A: F_b = (p_bottom - p_top)A = ρ_f g H A = ρ_f g V_disp.
(4) This derivation shows that the buoyant force depends only on the fluid density, the displaced volume, and g — not on the object’s material.

(5) If the object’s weight W = mg exceeds F_b, it sinks; if W < F_b, it accelerates upward until partially immersed, where displaced volume adjusts until F_b = W. Consider a solid iron cube of side 4 cm lowered into a…
The cube’s volume is 64\ cm^3 = 6.4×10^-5\ m^3.
Water density is 1000\ kg/m^3 and g = 9.8\ m/s^2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “buoyant force depends on the object’s density”) reveals the misconception that the material of the object determines the upward push, confusing weight with buoyancy.
remember: Define buoyant force and state the factors on which its magnitude depends.
Explain, using the concept of pressure variation with depth, why a submerged object experiences a net upward force.

cards.title: Archimedes’ principle states that any body wholly or partially immersed in a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Archimedes’ principle states that any body wholly or partially immersed in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal in magnitude to the weight of the fluid displaced by the body. Mathematically, F_b = ρ_f V_d g, where F_b is the buoyant force (N), ρ_f is the density of the fluid (kg m⁻³), V_d is the volume of fluid displaced (m³), and g is the acceleration due to gravity (9.8 m s⁻²). The principle links three sub‑concepts: (1) Buoyancy (the upward force itself, covered in node), (2) Pressure variation with depth (the cause of the net upward force, node), and (3) Floatation (the condition F_b = W for equilibrium, node). It also underpins the definition of relative density (ratio of a substance’s density to that of water at 4 °C, node). The principle applies to liquids and gases, provided the fluid is static and incompressible for the depth range considered.
steps: Archimedes’ principle tells us that the upward buoyant force on an immersed object equals the weight of the fluid it displaces.
Here is why: consider a solid cube of side L lowered gently into a beaker of water until it is fully submerged.
The water pressure on the bottom face is greater than on the top face because pressure increases with depth (p = p_0 + ρ_f g h).
The net upward force is the pressure difference times the area, which simplifies to ρ_f g L^3 — exactly the weight of water that would occupy the cube’s volume.

This reasoning holds for any shape because the fluid pressure acts normal to every surface element; integrating over the closed surface yields the same result: F_b = ρ_f V_d g. A practical Indian example: a steel katori…
If you crush the same katori into a solid ball, the displaced volume drops dramatically and the ball sinks.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “F_b = ρ_object V_object g”) reveals the misconception that the object’s own density determines the buoyant force, confusing weight of the object with weight of displaced fluid.
remember: State Archimedes’ principle in words and give the mathematical expression with symbols and SI units.

cards.title: Floatation is the state in which a body remains at rest on the surface of a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Floatation is the state in which a body remains at rest on the surface of a fluid, neither sinking nor rising. According to Archimedes’ principle, the upward buoyant force on a body immersed in a fluid equals the weight of the fluid displaced by the body. For floatation, the weight of the body ( W = m g = ρ_body V_body g ) must exactly balance this buoyant force ( F_b = ρ_fluid V_sub g ). Equating the two gives the quantitative condition ρ_body V_body = ρ_fluid V_sub, or the fraction of volume submerged V_sub/V_body = ρ_body/ρ_fluid. A body floats if its average density is less than or equal to the fluid density; it sinks if its density is greater. The concept links directly to the earlier nodes on pressure variation with depth, buoyancy, and Archimedes’ principle, and it sets the stage for the next node on density and relative density.
steps: The one thing to remember: A body floats when its weight equals the weight of the fluid it displaces, and the fraction submerged equals the ratio of the body’s density to the fluid’s density.
Here is why: 1.
Archimedes’ principle tells us the upward buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid. 2.
For a body at rest on the surface, net force is zero, so weight = buoyant force. 3.
Writing weight as ρ_body V_body g and buoyant force as ρ_fluid V_sub g, the g cancels, leaving ρ_body V_body = ρ_fluid V_sub. 4.
Rearranging gives V_sub/V_body = ρ_body/ρ_fluid — the fraction submerged depends only on densities. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “buoyant force is greater than weight”) reveals the misconception that floating requires a net upward force, confusing static equilibrium with upward acceleration.
remember: State the condition for a body to float in a fluid.
A solid sphere of density 800 kg/m³ is placed in a liquid of density 1000 kg/m³. Will it float? What fraction of its volume will be submerged.
A student says: “If a body floats, the buoyant force is greater than its weight.” Evaluate this statement.

cards.title: Density: the mass per unit volume of a substance, ρ = m/V
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Density: the mass per unit volume of a substance, ρ = m/V; SI unit kilogram per cubic metre (kg m⁻³), practical unit gram per cubic centimetre (g cm⁻³), with 1 g cm⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³. Representative values every numerical leans on: water 1000 kg m⁻³ (the anchor), ice 920, kerosene 800, mercury 13 600, aluminium 2700, iron 7800, copper 8900, gold 19 300, air ≈ 1.3. Determination routines: a REGULAR solid by geometry (weigh, measure sides, divide); an IRREGULAR solid insoluble in water by the measuring cylinder (immerse, read the volume rise — the displacement method) or a Eureka can; a LIQUID by the density bottle (a small flask with a ground-glass stopper carrying a fine capillary — filling it to the mark delivers a FIXED, repeatable volume, so density = (mass of liquid held)/(that volume)). Relative density (RD, specific gravity): the ratio of a substance's density to the density of water — RD = ρ_substance/ρ_water — a pure NUMBER with no units (two densities of the same kind divide their units away). Water at 4 °C (1000 kg m⁻³, its maximum density) is the standard. The two conversion bridges are permanently examinable: density = RD × 1000 kg m⁻³, and RD = density in g cm⁻³ (numerically identical, since water is 1 g cm⁻³). The loss-of-weight route (buoyancy converted into a measuring instrument, from/04_004): a solid heavier than and insoluble in water, weighing W₁ in air and W₂ fully immersed in water, satisfies RD = W₁/(W₁ − W₂) (both weighed in the same force units — gf or N — since the ratio cancels them); the density bottle's route for a liquid: RD = (mass of bottle+liquid − mass of bottle)/(mass of bottle+water − mass of bottle). The physical payoff is the float–sink decoder ('s condition in density language): a body sinks in a fluid if its density EXCEEDS the fluid's, floats if it is LESS (ice, 0.92 relative to water — floats with ≈ 92% of its volume buried; iron, 7.8 — sinks in water but floats in mercury, 13.6). Density inherits from mass and volume both their disciplines: mass in kg (g ÷ 1000), volume in m³ (cm³ × 10⁻⁶) BEFORE division, and the answer's units written every time.
steps: Density is packing; relative density is packing compared with water — and mastering this node means owning the number-to-number bridges (g cm⁻³ ↔ kg m⁻³ ↔ RD), the three measuring routines as reading-tables, and the…

Argument one: the definition is a division, and every error in the topic is an error in what the division was fed. ρ = m/V: feed it grams and cm³ and it answers in g cm⁻³ (iron: 78 g / 10 cm³ = 7.8 g cm⁻³); feed it…

The two answers are the SAME material saying its packing two ways, and the bridges are fixed exchange rates: ×1000 from g cm⁻³ to kg m⁻³, and RD equals the g cm⁻³ figure numerically because the standard (water) is…
The exam's favourite diet is mixed units — mass in grams, dimensions in centimetres, the answer demanded in kg m⁻³ — and the discipline is one-way: convert first, divide once, write the unit.

A density computed without its unit is a number, not a physics answer, and the marker's pencil knows it. Argument two: the three routines are reading-tables, and the density bottle is the exam's favourite.
Regular solid: weigh, measure (l × b × h), divide — geometry is the volume meter.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., RD = 8.9 g cm⁻³ (RD has NO units — attaching one is the topic's most-marked slip and the definition-question's direct target), ρ = 8900 g cm⁻³ (the ×1000 bridge applied to the wrong unit slot — the bridge converts g cm⁻³ UP to kg m⁻³…
remember: Recall: define density and relative density, state their SI (and CGS-practical) units, and write the two conversion….

cards.title: Relative density (RD) is the ratio of the density of a substance to the density…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Relative density (RD) is the ratio of the density of a substance to the density of water at 4 °C. It is a dimensionless quantity. Using Archimedes’ principle, the buoyant force on a body fully immersed in a fluid equals the weight of the fluid displaced. For a solid denser than water and insoluble in it, the loss of weight when immersed in water equals the weight of water displaced, which is proportional to the volume of the solid. Therefore, RD of the solid = weight in air ÷ (weight in air – weight in water). For a liquid, the same solid is weighed in air, in water, and in the liquid. The loss of weight in the liquid divided by the loss of weight in water gives the RD of the liquid: RD_liquid = (W_air – W_liquid) ÷ (W_air – W_water). This method links the concepts of density, buoyancy, and floatation without directly measuring volume.
steps: The relative density of a substance can be found by measuring its weight in air and its apparent weight when immersed in water (for solids) or by comparing the apparent loss of weight of a solid in the substance and in…
Here is why: first, Archimedes’ principle states that the upward buoyant force on an immersed body equals the weight of the fluid displaced.
Second, for a solid that sinks, the volume of water displaced equals the volume of the solid, so the loss of weight in water is directly proportional to the solid’s volume.

Third, because density is mass per unit volume, the ratio of the solid’s density to water’s density equals the ratio of its weight in air to the weight of water displaced, which is the loss of weight in water.
Fourth, for a liquid, the same solid displaces a different weight of liquid; the ratio of the two losses of weight gives the liquid’s relative density.
Consider a jeweller in Mumbai who wants to verify a gold ornament.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “kg/m³”) reveals the misconception that relative density carries the same unit as density, confusing a ratio with an absolute quantity.
remember: Define relative density and state its SI unit.
A solid weighs 50 N in air and 40 N in water. What is its relative density.
A student claims that the relative density of a liquid can be found by weighing the liquid directly on a balance. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: This node synthesizes the five core concepts of Chapter 4 Fluids…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: This node synthesizes the five core concepts of Chapter 4 Fluids: (1) Pressure in a fluid increases linearly with depth according to P = P_0 + ρ gh, where P_0 is atmospheric pressure, ρ is fluid density, g is acceleration due to gravity, and h is depth. (2) Buoyancy is the net upward force exerted by a fluid on an immersed body, equal to the weight of the displaced fluid. (3) Archimedes' principle states that the buoyant force on a body wholly or partially immersed in a fluid equals the weight of the fluid displaced. (4) Floatation occurs when the weight of a body equals the buoyant force; the body then displaces a volume of fluid whose weight matches its own weight. (5) Density ρ = m/V and relative density (specific gravity) RD = ρ_substance/ρ_water determine whether a body sinks or floats. These concepts are interlinked: pressure difference with depth creates buoyancy; Archimedes' principle quantifies it; floatation applies the principle to equilibrium; density and relative density provide the material property that decides the outcome. Mastery requires fluency in converting between these ideas and solving numerical problems that combine them.
steps: The single most important takeaway for the ICSE exam is that every fluid problem reduces to balancing forces and using the displaced-fluid weight as the buoyant force.
Here is why: (1) Pressure increases with depth, so the bottom of an immersed object feels a larger upward push than the top downward push — the net result is buoyancy.
(2) Archimedes' principle turns that net push into a simple rule: buoyant force = weight of displaced fluid.
(3) Floatation is just the special case where buoyant force equals object weight.
(4) Density and relative density let you decide floatation without measuring volume directly.
(5) CISCE questions often combine these steps: they give weight in air and apparent weight in water, expecting you to find relative density via loss of weight = buoyant force.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., P = ρ g h only) reveals the misconception that atmospheric pressure is negligible or already included in ρ g h — students forget that the fluid surface is exposed to the atmosphere and that gauge pressure excludes P_0.
remember: State the formula for pressure at a depth h in a fluid of density ρ, including atmospheric pressure P_0.

cards.title: Heat is energy in transit due to a temperature difference…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Heat is energy in transit due to a temperature difference; its SI unit is the joule (J). Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles, expressed in kelvin (K) or degree Celsius (°C). The chapter links these concepts to energy flow — conduction, convection, radiation — and to the anomalous expansion of water (maximum density at 4 °C). It classifies energy sources as renewable (solar, wind, biomass) and non‑renewable (coal, petroleum, natural gas). Finally, it explains the greenhouse effect: gases such as CO₂ and CH₄ trap outgoing infrared radiation, raising Earth’s average temperature — global warming. Each sub‑topic builds a framework for understanding energy use, environmental impact, and sustainable choices.
steps: The chapter is a roadmap that connects everyday heat experiences to global energy challenges.
Here is why: every cooking stove, refrigerator, and power plant illustrates the same physics — energy moving from hot to cold, changing forms, and affecting the environment.
Consider a pressure cooker: steam (heat) raises temperature, cooking food faster; the same principle drives turbines in a thermal power station.
Next, water’s anomalous expansion means ice floats, insulating lakes and allowing fish to survive — a unique property that shapes ecosystems in Himalayan streams.
Then, energy flow diagrams show how sunlight becomes chemical energy in plants, then food, then muscular work — a chain that underpins all life.
Renewable sources like solar panels on rooftops in Gujarat convert light directly to electricity, while non‑renewable coal in Jharkhand releases stored chemical energy but adds CO₂.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “calorie for heat and Celsius for temperature”) reveals the misconception that historical or non‑SI units are the standard in modern physics.
remember: State the SI unit of heat and the SI unit of temperature.
Explain why heat and temperature are not the same, using the particle model.
A student claims that water contracts continuously as it cools from 10 °C to 0 °C. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Heat is a form of energy that flows spontaneously from a body at a higher…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Heat is a form of energy that flows spontaneously from a body at a higher temperature to a body at a lower temperature, and ceases to flow the moment the two bodies reach the same temperature. Because heat is energy, its SI unit is the joule (J); the older CGS unit is the calorie (cal), defined as the heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 g of water by 1 °C, with the bridge 1 cal = 4.186 J ≈ 4.2 J and 1 kilocalorie (kcal) = 1000 cal = 4186 J. Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body — the physical property that measures the average kinetic energy of its particles and, crucially, determines the direction of heat flow. Its SI unit is the kelvin (K); everyday scales are the Celsius (°C) and Fahrenheit (°F) scales. The three scales are fixed to the same two calibration points — the freezing point and boiling point of pure water at normal atmospheric pressure: 0 °C = 32 °F = 273.15 K (ICSE working value 273 K) and 100 °C = 212 °F = 373.15 K. Between these points the Celsius scale has 100 divisions, the Fahrenheit 180, so one Celsius degree spans 1.8 Fahrenheit degrees. The conversion bridges are F = (9/5)C + 32, C = (5/9)(F − 32) and T(K) = t(°C) + 273.15. The lowest possible temperature, at which particle kinetic energy is at its minimum, is absolute zero: 0 K = −273.15 °C — no body can be colder. When two bodies in contact stop exchanging heat they are in thermal equilibrium — they have the same temperature; a thermometer works precisely because, given enough contact time, it reaches thermal equilibrium with the body it measures (the reading is meaningful only then). Heat is a cause; temperature is an effect: heat is energy in transit, while temperature is the state-variable that survives after the transfer has stopped. The amount of heat a body can hold depends on its mass, the change of temperature it undergoes, and the nature of the substance — which is why equal temperatures do not imply equal heat, and why the distinction is examined year after year.
steps: Heat and temperature are two different currencies — temperature is the intensity that decides the direction of flow, heat is the quantity that actually moves — and every instrument and formula in this node exists to…
Argument one: the direction rule and its logic.
Particles of every body are in ceaseless motion; temperature measures the average kinetic energy of that motion.

When a hot body touches a cold body, fast particles at the interface keep colliding with slow ones, and on average the fast ones lose energy while the slow ones gain — so energy flows from higher temperature to lower…
This is why heat is defined as energy in transit — once transfer has finished, the energy is simply internal energy of the body, and "heat flows from temperature" is the only allowed sentence;
"cold flows in" is forbidden, since coldness is not a substance.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., defining heat as "the hotness of a body" (that is temperature's job — the definition mark pays for the words "energy that flows"; a heat-less definition collapses the whole distinction the chapter examines), (b) 293 + 273 = 566 °C (the…

Reasoning: (P) Convert 68 °F to °C and to K. (Q) A weather report says Delhi touched 40 °C; express this in….

cards.title: Anomalous expansion of water is the unique thermal behaviour where liquid water…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Anomalous expansion of water is the unique thermal behaviour where liquid water contracts on cooling from 0 °C to 4 °C, reaching its maximum density (≈ 1000 kg m⁻³) at 4 °C, and then expands on further cooling to 0 °C and on heating above 4 °C. Unlike most substances, whose volume decreases monotonically with temperature, water’s coefficient of volume expansion β is negative between 0 °C and 4 °C and positive elsewhere. This inversion arises from hydrogen‑bond restructuring: as temperature falls, molecules form a more open tetrahedral network that occupies less volume until 4 °C, after which the network expands. The phenomenon governs lake stratification, ice flotation, and the mechanical stress on containers and pipes during freezing. It is quantitatively described by the temperature‑dependent density ρ(T) with a maximum at T = 4 °C, and by the volume‑temperature relation V = V₀[1 + β(T − 4)²] for small deviations, where β changes sign at 4 °C.
steps: Water’s density peaks at 4 °C, making it contract on cooling from 0 °C to 4 °C and expand on either side of this temperature.

Here is why: as water cools, hydrogen bonds pull molecules into a tighter, more ordered arrangement until 4 °C; below that, the same bonds force an open hexagonal lattice that occupies more space, so volume increases…
Consider a lake in Shimla in December.
Surface water cools first, becomes denser, and sinks until the whole lake reaches 4 °C.
Further cooling makes the surface layer lighter, so it stays on top and freezes, forming an insulating ice sheet.
This stratification protects aquatic life.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “0 °C” or “100 °C”) reveals the misconception that water behaves like most liquids, whose density rises continuously on cooling.
remember: State the temperature at which pure water has its maximum density and give its approximate value in SI units.
